subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in addition to what I said the other evening, now that development is being carried on all over Canada in regard to water-powers, minerals and oil lands, it is more than ever necessary that the house adopt as a principle the spirit of the resolution. It is only a few years ago since the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario, which at present is furnishing a precedent to the whole world in the matter of power supply at cost, had to purchase those valuable water rights at enormous cost. The plant and water rights at Niagara falls had to be purchased from a private corporation. This was property that had been alienated from the people for a mere trifle. The natural resources such as coal, for example, should never have been allowed to fall into private hands, but should have been developed in the interests of the people. New Zealand furnishes a splendid example in that respect. That country owns and operates several of the mines in New Zealand, and the people there are getting their coal at cost price.
To come back to the principle of the resolution, when I first went to western Canada and settled near Saskatoon, I found that the Dominion government had granted some two million acres of land around what is now the city of Saskatoon to what was known then as the Temperance Colonization Society. I had in consequence to go further back from the railroad than otherwise would have been necessary because all the free homesteads between where I settled and the railway had been taken up. This large tract of land that I speak of was given away practically for a song, and under the agreement which

Natural Resources-Mr. Evans
the society had with the government, they had to locate a settler on each section of land within three years. They brought out a good many ne'er-do-wells from Ontario-

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
It is quite true, Mr. Speaker, that there were still a good many left behind. I believe that most of them who came out there were ministers' sons, but that does not count. At all events, after they had exhausted the little loan which the society was allowed to advance to them, they simply pulled up stakes and went away, and any of us who acquired one of those homesteads had to pay five hundred dollars or so, or go further out.
Even after 1896 the same practice continued, but on a much larger scale. This gave rise to suspicion, and a great many of our government heads at that time were brought under suspicion. The Saskatchewan Valley Land Company was a case in point where a tract of land comprising almost as much as an empire was given away. They only paid one dollar per acre for the land, and they were also given the privilege of selling at an enhanced price by giving the settler a free homestead alongside-a privilege which they got from the federal government. Immense areas were disposed of in that way.
When confederation was first mooted, the railway question was the chief problem of government. Indeed, sir, it seems to be still a thorny problem for this government, although our financial ability to cope with it is much greater now than it was then. One of the conditions of the provinces uniting was that a transcontinental railway should be built, and I want to point out that the burden of the construction of this great highway fell particularly on western Canada. The government gave away land that amounted in value, I believe, to more than the whole plant of the Canadian Pacific Railway was worth at any time. The west was not able to, defend itself at that time against these injustices, and the whole burden of industry and railway construction fell practically on that part of Canada. Every transcontinental line was built "for the people of the west," to let the politicians tell the tale. The people of the maritime provinces were not even content with a railway which gave them connection with the rest of Canada. Ontario got railways built through a wilderness as big as an empire, at the expense of the people of western Canada. It was really the farmer, with his wife and family, who by sweated 
labour had to pay the taxes on a billion dollars' worth of land in order to construct roads to get at the sidings of the Canadian Pacific at that time, and to construct schools for their own use.
Since then, this problem has been intensified by the granting of water-powers to private interests, and this has brought another set of privilege seekers to parliament asking favours in this respect. It is very likely- this is more than a guess on my part-that campaign funds are furnished sufficient to elect the henchmen they can trust in this respect. One would think that Canadian statesmen of to-day would hurry to settle this vexed question, and relieve themselves from any suspicion that might arise in the matter of the disposal of these water-power sites and other natural resources. Not only has the great water-power site of the Seven Sisters falls in Manitoba been disposed of, but the great riches of the Flin-Flon areas are now to be exploited for twenty-five years without the people getting any benefit from their God-given resources. The people in that case are simply being plundered, robbed of their own possessions, and this is being done without making any exaction of the company as to permanency of employment, or even as to the rate of wages to be paid in that area.

I was going to say that not long hence labour troubles will arise, expenses will be created, and then what? All I can say is that we are increasing the vote each year for the militia and defence. Troubles are

Natural Resources-Mr. Emns
going to arise in those areas, just as they have done with the British Empire Steel Company, and how are you going to settle them? The west is still bearing the burden of all these things, as well as the burden of the railway construction which formed the basis of confederation, and yet freight rates are higher in western Canada to-day than in any other part of the country. At confederation there was practically no sentiment for union in the maritime provinces or in the other provinces. It was virtually a case of necessity. I question whether to-day there is very much national unity to be found in this Dominion. I go further, Mr. Speaker. The way things are, and judging by the legislation emanating from this house, in all seriousness I say there is not much of a spirit of Canadian unity exhibited here. It does seem to me that the part played by certain areas through their representation in this house is simply a case of grab and grab -get what you can. The Duncan commission was clearly the outcome of party expediency. Its recommendations were carried out for the same reason. Coming back to the west, I understand that by an agreement between the Dominion government, the Alberta government and the Hudson's Bay Company, the company agreed to release certain areas of land in that province, to be later selected from a list that the Minister of the Interior would furnish to the company. Where are these lands to be located? In Saskatchewan? If that is true, it simply gives a clue to the reason for dealing with one province at a time, and the injustice will still be perpetuated against Saskatchewan.
On page 583 of Hansard, in referring to the conferences held by the Dominion government with representatives of the provincial governments, the Prime Minister is reported as follows:
This government took the position that the right thing to do was to say that we believed the western provinces should be put as nearly as possible in exactly the position they would hav* been in had they hald their resources from the moment they were created as provinces.
Now, the conditions prevailing at the time that these provinces received partial autonomy in 1905 have nothing to do with the conditions on which they should receive their natural resources to-day. The constitution of Canada, the British North America Act, provides explicitly for just such conditions. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta never entered the union as provinces; they were carved out of
an area known as Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territories. These entities entered the Dominion in 1870 by an imperial order in council dated June 23 of that year. It was passed at the request of the Dominion government, which presented an address to Her Majesty requesting that this be done. At that time the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Quebec never made any claim whatsoever to any of the natural resources, they never suggested that Rupert's Land or the Northwest Territories ever belonged to the original confederation. The claim put forward the other day by the member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) and other members from the maritime provinces that they had a proprietary right in the natural resources of western Canada would apply just as well to any part of Australia or to any of the territories in South Africa.
Instead of carrying out its trust obligations, the federal parliament in 1872 passed the Dominion Lands Act, by which it appropriated to itself the lands of these new members of the confederation. The rights of these provinces in the matter of their public domain, minerals, water-powers, timber areas, grazing leases, fisheries, and so on, and their rights in regard to education and taxation were defined by the imperial order in council to which I have referred. The Dominion Lands Act ousted these new members from their rightful place in the confederation. The return of their property now must be made on the basis of the imperial order in council of June 23, 1870, when Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territories entered the union as free entities and were entitled to all their rights and possessions just the same as any of the older provinces.
Now, if Rupert's Land and1 the Northwest Territories entered confederation at that time, no denominational rights then existed in those territories.
It was also provided under section 118 of the British North America Act that a subsidy should be paid by the Dominion government to the several provinces for the support of their governments and legislatures. Canada also assumed the debts of the provinces that entered confederation at that time. So it would seem that Rupert's Land and the Northwest Territories entered the Dominion on much more favourable terms than any other province.	.
But this is what I should like to impress on the government now. We must be a confederation of states united by unmistakable

Natural. Resources-Mr. McPherson
constitutional rights or we shall become a series of colonies, more diverse and unrelated as time goes on. I say the Dominion must stop meddling in what is purely local provincial affairs, and I say further that equality of status is the only real 'basis of union.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention when this debate opened to take part in it, but as it proceeded it became noticeable that the original resolution hardly met with the approval of any section of this house. In fact the mover of the resolution recognized this himself in his opening remarks. Afterwards an amendment was moved, the effect of which was to confine the purpose of the resolution to waterpowers.
The major portion of the debate has not centered around the resolution or the amendment in its widest sense but has been restricted to a subject which is now pretty well understood in this house, namely, the disposal of the Seven Sisters water site in the province of Manitoba. Now, discussing the amendment last Thursday, the mover of the original resolution (Mr. Woodsworth) made a few remarks which I think necessitate my stepping into the debate as a member from Manitoba, and especially to put on record my own views and actions in connection with the Seven Sisters discussion. The hon. member's statement, made on February 28, 1929, is found at page 571 of Hansard. It reads:
I charged that the action of the government was a violation of solemn assurance made to the Manitoba members. This point has been fairly well covered during the course of the discussion. We were told that we would be consulted; I ask if any member of this house says we were consulted when all that has been brought out is that of seventeen members seven were called together in Winnipeg, and the rest of us were not in any way notified.
That statement makes it necessary for me to explain my own position. I cannot agree with the mover of the resolution; although I was not one of the seven members who attended the meeting referred to-in fact I never heard of it until I came to the house- I was consulted by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). I may say that my attention was first called to the problem in Manitoba by an article which appeared in the Winnipeg papers, both the Free Press and the Tribune, on the third and fourth days of February last. I shall quote only the article from the Tribune, inasmuch as there is very little difference between the two newspapers so far as the news report is concerned. In the Winnipeg Tribune of February 4 the following appears:

In answer to a question of Mr. Farmer, M.L. A., Premier Bracken read a telegram sent Thursday to the Hon. Charles Stewart, Minister of the Interior, in which he requested no action be taken in connection with any lease grant which would prejudice the province's application for the site made more than two years ago.
The government, he said, would strongly object to any commitments being made in favour of a private company.
The impression I received, not so much from that telegram as from the discussion in the house, was that the provincial government at that time had in mind the obtaining of this site for the purpose of developing it themselves in connection with their hydroelectric system throughout the province, from Winnipeg west and southwest. And I heartily agreed with them in retaining it if they thought that they could develop it economically as a part of their system. For that reason I signed the document, which has been referred to by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), along with other members of the house, asking the Minister of the Interior not to dispose of the site but to retain it for the purposes of the provincial government; and in that document there were added the words, "For the purpose of development with the hydro-electric system".
The hon. member for Nelson .stated that we had signed a round robin. I would point out that, like the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden), I nearly rose to my feet to object to this statement, because I have no recollection of signing such a document. I do not think for a moment that the hon. member when making that statement intended to mislead the house; I am absolutely satisfied that he did not. But it is only fair to direct the attention of the house to the fact that the execution and signing of a round robin is an entirely different thing from an instrument signed in the ordinary way. A round robin, as I understand it-and this I think is the impression which generally prevails-is a document signed in a circle in order to hide the identity of the person who raises the question, when there is some doubt as to whether that person should be known or not. Such a person is rather asbamed of his action. Now, there was nothing like that in connection with this document. I do not know where I came on the list, but I presume it was signed as submitted to the various members. This document asked that the site be retained for the purpose of the provincial government in connection with their hydro development, and if that government wanted it for that purpose I was personally pre-

Natural Resources-Mr. McPherson
pared that they should have it. It was purely a question of busmen whether it could be logically and economically developed by them.
I had a good deal to do with the provincial hydro-electric in Manitoba; in fact, I was a member of the legislature at the time it was started, the government having previously purchased power from the Winnipeg power plant. As to whether they could develop this site or not, is I think, a question which we need not discuss to any extent; and as to whether they entered into a reasonable agreement, I am not very much concerned at the moment. That is a question which we in Manitoba will dispose of when the necessity arises, and the opinion of the province as a whole will, I think, ultimately prevail. But so far as we are concerned here, the fact remains that when I left Ottawa I left with the impression that the Minister of the Interior would consult me in some way before there was any definite disposition of the power site to the province in any form, either directly or indirectly. And I may say right now that the minister, so far as I am personally concerned, fulfilled his obligation to the limit. I met the minister in Winnipeg; I have forgotten the date, but it -was the day he arrived from the east, while the Dominion-provincial conference was being held in Ottawa in connection with natural resources. He told me then that he had left the conference in session and that he expected there would be an arrangement whereby the natural resources would be turned over to the province of Manitoba. In view of that situation he asked me what my attitude would be towards the lease of the Seven Sisters. Now my nationality makes me cautious, and I told the minister that I should much prefer waiting until I knew what the terms were before I gave a decided opinion on the matter. A few days or a week afterwards the terms on which the province was to obtain its natural resources became public property, and some time between that and the 10th of August I sent word to the minister that in view of the fact that the natural resources agreement had been amicably settled between the province and the Dominion I personally could see no reason for pressing my views regarding one item of the resources for the purpose of blocking the whole deal. And I withdrew my opposition to the execution of the lease, with one proviso only, namely, that there must be no mistake, if the lease were given to the private company, that it would have to be given on the request of the provincial government and in such a way that there could be no doubt about it, and that the provincial
government would have to assume the whole responsibility. On that ground I withdrew my objection. It is only fair to the minister to make this statement. I never saw him afterwards; I was not at the meeting.
Now as to the resolution as a whole, my reasons for opposing it are, I think, based on good grounds. Ever since I can remember, the province of Manitoba has been demanding the return of its natural resources. That and the Hudson Bay railway had been the two great war cries out there as long as I could remember. We have settled the one, and the other is now in shape to be settled. I personally have supported resolutions demanding the return of these natural resources when such resolutions have come up in the local house while I was a member. I did not think it my duty to interfere in any way with the completion of that deal, which has been so long in coming; to me it was not a hurried affair but the result of years of conferences and negotiations, and it could not be concluded too soon.
The effect of the transfer will be to give us complete control, but I cannot quite understand why the amendment has been proposed. I do not see why, if the original resolution was too broad, they should pick upon the water-powers as the one resource which should be retained under the control of this parliament, and there are two reasons whj' I cannot understand that. The first reason is to a certain extent a matter of record, and I want to read a few words of the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George (Mr. Cahan), delivered in this house on April 19, 1926, and found at page 2569 of Hansard. We were discussing water-powers, and the hon. member said:
It is true that we have vested in the crown, as represented by the Dominion government, large water^powers in the territories which undoubtedly are soon to be vested in the several provincial legislatures, but I will say that 1 do not believe any department of the Dominion government is more honestly and more efficiently managed, supervised and controlled than is the water-powers branch.
That was the opinion expressed by one of the leading members of the official opposition, a gentleman eminently fair in debate, regardless of whether or not we agree with his views. The peculiar situation which arises is that following that statement the mover of this present resolution (Mr. Woodsworth) said:
I quite agree.
I have no doubt the Minister of the Interior will agree with the member for St. Lawrence-St. George, so we have the unique situation of members on this side of the house agreeing

Natural Resources-Mr. McPherson
with one of the outstanding members of the opposition and with the mover of this resolution that the water-powers branch is one of the most efficiently managed departments of the government, yet this is the one department which it is desired to put under the control of this house.
Then there is another peculiar situation. I could understand the situation more easily if the amendment had dealt with mines instead of water-powers; as a rule mining is an industry which is developed in a very small way at first. A prospector goes out and makes his location and if he can interest capital the property is developed. The location of a mine has very little to do with its development, if it is rich enough, but the development of water-powers is quite different. Water-powers must foe developed by large corporations or by governments, because the amount of money necessary for such development is very large. In addition, there is no immediate return as there is from a mine; they must depend upon the demand for power, and usually that demand is not nearly sufficient to utilize the initial output of the development, so the people interested in a waterpower development must take means to create a. demand which will utilize the output of that development to its fullest capacity. That means a good deal of work; it is more or less of a speculative proposition and necessitates a large amount of detail work in the way of business management. The amendment to the resolution has been proposed by a representative from the province of Ontario, and I would like to point out that the provinces of Ontario and Quebec have great waterpower resources which have been developed to a large extent. When the province of Manitoba undertakes the development of its water-powers, either through private corporations or under public ownership, it comes in direct competition with the provinces of Ontario and Quebec from an industrial point of view, and the result of this amended resolution would be to give the representatives of competing provinces a control over the development of water-powers in the province of Manitoba. I object to that from the very start, Mr. Speaker; I think it is fundamentally unsound. No matter how honest they may be-and I am not questioning their integrity for a moment-I would consider it poor business if I had to operate a business under the control of an active competitor.
The province of Manitoba has been demanding the return of these water powers, and now the government have entered into an agreement to return not only the Water powers but 
the rest of the natural resources as well. Speaking as a member from the province of Manitoba I strongly object to the resolution both in its original form and as amended. I claim that Manitoba is not still in swaddling clothes; we have grown up. We have waited a long time for the return of these resources, and while some hon. members have expressed doubt as to whether Manitoba can be relied upon upon to exercise proper judgment in the development and disposition of the natural resources, I believe we have >the average, if not better than^the average, class of legislators, and whether the government be Conservative, Liberal, Progressive or Labour, if that government does not use good judgment and carry on the business properly it will get its deserts at the hands of the electors of that province. I want to leave the disposition, management and control of our natural resources in our own hands, and we in Manitoba will be willing to take full responsibility for their proper administration. For that reason I strenuously object to this resolution, which says in effect, "You are not capable of managing your own business."

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the Prime Minister is not in his seat; he debated this resolution and amendment for a couple of hours and then stated that he thought the discussion had lasted long enough. However, statements made by the Prime Minister render it necessary for me to attempt to convince the house that they are not in accordance with the facts, especially with regard to what the Prime Minister said would be the result if this amendment were adopted, namely, a conflict between eastern and western Canada and the failure to allow the prairie provinces to develop their own resources.
In the first place I feel it necessary to say that the stricture which was passed upon my leader by the Prime Minister is wholly incorrect. The Prime Minister charged that my leader and we on this side of the house were not in favour of a speedy return of these resources, but that statement is not borne out by the facts. Anyone who will read Hansard will see that my leader was referring to the situation created by the Minister of the Interior himself in relation to the Seven Sisters falls. If a tramp who is loitering along the highway suddenly starts to run you naturally want to know the reason for all the hurry, and in any case my leader did not have before him the letter of June 7, which followed the statement made in this house by the minister on June 6.

Natural Resources-Mr. Ryckman
I desire to discuss this matter apart from any consideration of the Seven Sisters power site, as I understand that is something we cannot recover. We have an amendment before us which, in my opinion is sound, good business and within the proper exercise of the discretion of this house. I do not think anyone will say that an important asset such as water-powers should be disposed of by cabinet control and not by the control of parliament. The Prime Minister was of the same mind on February 9, 1924, as appears by the letter which he placed on Hansard, and if we relate the amendment back to the transfer of the natural resources to Manitoba we find that the Prime Minister thought the approval of this house necessary to such a transfer. I am opposed, and I believe other members of this house are opposed, to the alienation of important assets without the consent of parliament. It is admitted by everyone that water-powers are amongst the most valuable assets that the Dominion or the provinces have, and that they should be alienated by a body of men or by the Minister of the Interior, as happened in the case of the Seven Sisters falls, is something to which the people of this country will not submit. It is the opinion of some members of this house that a mistake has been made with regard to this particular water-power site, but I belive it is the unanimous opinion that if the house or the provincial house is to deal with the water-powers of the Dominion or of the province it should be carried out according to some plan which is well understood by parliament, and one in which parliament has the final word. The Prime Minister said that in this case it would relate to only the three prairie provinces; that Ontario and Quebec would not be concerned and that the only control the Dominion had was in relation to the water-powers of the three prairie provinces. I think it is necessary that the Prime Minister should read the British North America Act again, and I think he should consider the water-powers within the railway belt in British Columbia. The question of the disposition of the water-powers of the 'Georgian bay and communicating streams was before this house, I believe two years ago. There is also the question of the Carillon falls, in which the people of Canada are interested.
One thing that surprises me is that not one word has been stated in this debate as to the claim the Prime Minister made as recently as the month of October when a factum was presented on behalf of his government claiming that the Dominion of Canada had control over every water-power in any navigable water in Canada. Navigable water means
navigable in fact, but what does navigable in fact mean? It does not mean that it shall be necesary that a Mauretania can ply through the waters, that some river boat shall find passage, or even a rowboat, but it means the waters where a lone Indian in his canoe can pass and re-pass-that is navigation in fact.
I have before me the brief on the reference which was made to the Supreme Court of Canada, the brief out of which His Lordship the Chief Justice of the supreme court said he did not think anything could have been left. This brief is signed on behalf of the Attorney General of Canada; it is signed Lucien Cannon, N. W. Rowell, Charles Laur-endeau, H. J. Symington, C. P. Plaxton and Vincent C. MacDonald. The claim was made on behalf of the government of the Prime Minister that in any water navigable in fact, such as I have described-if my description is not considered as being correct I will read the long definition appearing in this factum of the Attorney General-in such a stream controlled by the Dominion government, the Dominion government controlled all waterpower and could expropriate it without compensation and go into the business of generating and disposing of electrical power.

It cannot be said that there is anything out of the way when the claim is made that the house should seek to exercise control over such powers, large and important as they are. That is the purport of the amendment. As to the question of dividing east from west, to drag in an argument of that kind in a case such as this is beneath the contempt of the house. There is no question of east and west being separated over a matter of this kind. The east, as I understand it, is unanimously in favour of the west receiving its resources and administering those resources in the interests of the provinces themselves and not, I may say, in the interest of the Dominion government, as was the position taken before the supreme court.
The agreement reached with Manitoba contemplated the approval of parliament, and I wish to refer briefly to this. Just exactly what the agreement was between the federal government and the government of Manitoba I do not think has been given to the house except in the statement which refers to the conference that was held and which appears on page 518 of Hansard. The fourth paragraph reads:
The findings of the commission to be submitted to the parliament of Canada and to the legislature of Manitoba.
I wish to direct attention to the fifth paragraph :
Upon agreement on the financial terms following consideration of the report of the commission, the respective governments to introduce the necessary legislation to give effect to the financial terms as agreed upon, and to effect the transfer to the province of the unalienated natural resources within its boundaries, subject to any trust existing in respect thereof, and without prejudice to any interest other than that of the crown in the same.
Paragraph five provided that the parliament of Canada and the legislature of Manitoba should ratify the terms of the transfer to the province of its unalienated natural resources. Paragraph six was just a working paragraph, in the interim providing for ordinary business. The transfer of the Seven Sisters falls, a transfer of such immense importance which fixed upon the province the question of public or private ownership for thirty years, was one that was not contemplated without the authorization of the provincial legislature or the approval of parliament.

speechtext:
What did take place?
It has been stated that Manitoba could not have done this itself. I think it could and just in this way. Manitoba could have accepted the lease in this case in all its terms just in the same way as it could accept any other benefit. It could have made a simple assignment of the property in the lease and directed it towards that company. But the government most unwisely undertook to do for Manitoba what Manitoba could not do itself because it did not have the approval of its people and of its legislature. That is plainly the situation. If that approval had been obtained, all the trouble, doubt and suspicion to which the Frime Minister has referred would have been avoided. If there was not something sinister, it is strange that paragraph six should be in the terms in which it is. What is the result? As admitted by every hon. member there is a large question of provincial policy, that of public or private ownership. This has been decided for Manitoba by the federal government and the Bracken government without the people of Manitoba having had an opportunity to express their will. Private ownership has been fastened on Manitoba for at least thirty years and perhaps for all time, and this has been done, as has been shown, without the approval of the members of the house. That is, the action of the federal government has been taken without the members interested having had an opportunity to express their opinion upon the matter, and a great deal of explaining is necessary as to why, when the matter was up for consideration, no chance was given to consult either the legislature or the people of Manitoba. As regards the members of this house who were interested, I think they have been put into a bag, tied up like blind kittens and dropped over the Seven Sisters falls. I am anxious that it will be impossible for such a situation ever to occur again. Therefore, why not let us pass a resolution of this kind saying that when it is the intention to dispose
of such important natural resources as water-powers, the house, if it has control over those water-powers, shall have a say in the disposition of them? Years ago many now sitting on that side of the house stood, when on this side of the house, for that very thing-no alienation of the important assets of the Dominion without the consent of parliament. Even the present Prime Minister then declared that parliament should speak, that the government of this country should be by parliament, and not by the few, that the members of parliament, whether of his party or of any other party, should have the opportunity to express their will. But the Prime Minister now says that he is asked to break an agreement. He is not asked to break an agreement. There is no such question raised in the amendment to the resolution.
Let me point out to the Prime Minister what actually has occurred in an other case. His government by order in council authorized the execution of a contract with Sir William Petersen. That agreement was subject to the ratification of parliament. That contract was, if I may use the word, a most unworthy contract, having regard to the needs of the people of this country. Instead of giving, as it purported to give, lower ocean freight rates to the shippers of this country, it gave control of rates to Sir William Petersen, and when that was found out, parliament did not ratify the contract. Canada receded. The name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Hon. Mr. Low, was on that contract. The contract had been authorized by the government and by the right hon. the Prime Minister, but the government receded from that contract which it had authorized. The government could have forced it through the house if it had so desired, but the result would have been a contract which was not in the interests of Canada. Parliament had its chance, and parliament saved the situation. If this amendment passes, parliament will have the chance to save the situation again.

speechtext:
I am for public ownership; I believe in it, but I am not blindfolded by it. I am convinced that if Premier Bracken had gone into the development of the Seven Sisters falls he would have killed public ownership in the province of Manitoba for ever, because it was proved beyond1 a doubt in the report of one of the most competent engineers, Dr. Hogg, who is renowned in Ontario for his integrity, and whose authority I think no one will question, that the development of the Seven Sisters power site as a provincial enterprise was a folly economically.
Here was the situation. We needed power in Manitoba, and the Seven Sisters was the first power site that should be developed. The provincial government in Manitoba entered into a contract with the Winnipeg Electric Company. That was one of the best

contracts that ever was made by any province with a private corporation. It was the most water-tight contract possible, with the public protected in every way, shape and form. The Manitoba government said: We will withdraw our application for this lease if you will sign that contract ; and the Winnipeg Electric Company signed the contract.
What does that contract mean? It means getting closer to public ownership than we would ever have done had the cantract not been made. Why? Because it eliminates one of the greatest obstacles in the way of the development of power on the Winnipeg river. It wipes out the perpetual rights which the Winnipeg Electric Company enjoyed on the Pinawa channel. It increases the development of power on the Winnipeg river by between fifty and sixty thousand horse-power. In addition, the provincial government at the end of thirty years have the right to expropriate the development on a cost basis, less depreciation, the cost to be arrived at by the engineers of the water-powers branch, who are on the works at the time of construction, and the engineers of the Winnipeg Electric Company, and if they fail to agree, the question is to be referred to the exchequer court, whose decision shall be final.
So I say that the provincial government made a good contract for the people of Manitoba, and I am positive that when the political turmoil in the province of Manitoba is over, and the people of Manitoba have had a chance to find out what is in that contract, Premier Bracken will go down in the history of the province as having made one of the best deals that ever was made for the people of Manitoba. That is my opinion. Not only is Premier Bracken to be congratulated, but the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and all his colleagues are to be congratulated, first, because they have placed Manitoba in a position where we are going to get our natural resources in a very short time. Even if we do not get them within a year or two, in the meantime they will be administered by the federal authorities in accordance with the wishes of the province of Manitoba. I wish to congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister and his colleagues on bringing the agreement so close to completion in July last.
My hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Ryckman) asked: Instead of granting the lease of the Seven Sisters power site to the Winnipeg Electric Company, why did not the Minister of the Interior lease it to the Manitoba government? Well, I am not

Natural Resources-Mr. Adshead
a lawyer-don't want to be-but my understanding is that until the resources are actually transferred to Manitoba the Minister of the Interior had no other course open, he simply had to grant the lease as requested by the Manitoba government. I congratulate him on the fact that in this lease from the water-powers branch to the Winnipeg Electric Company the interests of the public are better safeguarded than in any similar lease within my knowledge or, I think, within the knowledge of most hon. members.
But, Mr. Speaker, we are in a most extraordinary position. My hon. friend from Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) the other night when the amendment was moved by the acting leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) said: Since it mentions water-powers I can vote for the amendment. How is he going to reconcile his attitude with the resolution which he had on the order paper for two sessions to my knowledge, and which this house passed unanimously the other day for the return of the natural resources to the prairie provinces without any restrictions? Are we now going to say: Four or five days ago we did not know what we were doing; we want to put restrictions on the return of those resources. I have said before and I repeat my statement, that this resolution and the amendment thereto affect the three prairie provinces and no others. The maritime provinces, Quebec and Ontario have always handled their natural resources. I say to my hon. friends opposite from the province of Ontario, who to-day are trying to convince the public that they are so much concerned over public ownership in Manitoba, that all the water-powers in northern Ontario were given to private corporations by order in council. And' rightly so, because if the Ontario government had waited for the local legislature to approve of the contracts the development of that great northern country would have been retarded, and Canada would have been the loser.
Let us be fair, Mr. Speaker. Western Canada has been fighting for the return of its natural resources ever since I have been in that country, which is close on fifty years. Manitoba has been a member of confederation since 1870, but she has never had control of her natural resources. We in Manitoba can handle our own affairs, we are just as intelligent as our fellow-Canadians in the sister provinces. I for one will not be a party to having any outside authority say what we in western Canada shall do with our natural 78594-40
resources. Therefore I intend to vote against the resolution and the amendment, and to oppose with all my strength any proposal tending to restrict the development of western Canada.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am a disinterested spectator of what has been going on between the Manitoba government and the members from that province and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). The resolution deals with the control of parliament over the disposition of the natural resources now administered by the federal government, but the discussion has developed into an attack on the Minister of the Interior for his alleged breach of faith with eighteen of the Manitoba members with respect to the leasing of the Seven Sisters falls power site. In fact at one stage the attack became so severe that you, sir, had to call some hon. members to order for challenging statements made by the minister.
Now as to the dispute, I have not much to say. The order in council dealing with the power site was signed on August 1, 1928. It says:
Pending this transfer-
That is, completion of the agreement between the government of Manitoba and the Dominion government.
-the policy of the government of Canada in the administration of the natural resources of Manitoba to be in accord with the washes of the government of the province of Manitoba.
From that very date the power of the Minister of the Interior to administer those resources was subject entirely to the wishes of the provincial government. It has been argued that the minister should not have taken- final action until the provincial legislature had passed upon the action of the Bracken government. I do not think that is the real situation. I believe that the government of Manitoba was appointed by the legislature as its agents, and as such the provincial government are responsible to the legislature, and to no other legislative authority.
I know in the province of Alberta the Minister of the Interior on one occasion was criticized for having granted a license for hydro-electric power to the Calgary Power Company without having consulted the premier, Mr. Brownlee; but afterwards it was found out that he had done so. At once the criticism of the United Farmers of Alberta was directed at Premier Brownlee

626	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Motherwell
Looking through the press of Manitoba, I find that even those papers that are averse to the granting of the lease to the Winnipeg Electric Company do not criticize the Minister of the Interior, but Premier Bracken and his government. Therefore I cannot vote in favour of the resolution or the amendment. As has been said, the resolution is double-barrelled. It may be said: If you vote against this resolution or against the amendment the people of Calgary will think you are opposed to public ownership. On the other hand, by voting in favour I may be charged with a desire to perpetuate the control by the federal authorities of the natural resources of the western provinces. But I am quite satisfied that if the resolution and amendment carry it will be inferred not only in this house but throughout the Dominion to be a vote of censure on the Minister of the Interior. Therefore having reached the conclusion that under the agreement between Manitoba and the Dominion he could have taken no other course than comply with the wishes of the provincial government, I can support neither the resolution nor the amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution
would seem to be the result of certain political backfire investigations that have been preceding in the province of Manitoba for some time. It is not so apparent, however, just what the meaning of the resolution and the amendment is, judging from the wide scope of the discussion and the many interpretations put upon them.
Taking the interpretation of the hon. sponsor of the resolution, I gather that he does not desire to raise the question as to the respective merits of private ownership of power and public ownership; nor does he wish to discuss the merits or demerits of the bargain itself. He is of the opinion that the lease is an exceedingly good one, prepared under an act which possibly is not excelled in any part of the world. So that we are reduced to this interpretation of the matter, from the standpoint of the hon. gentleman, that he raises the question as to whether any further alienation of our resources in the west-not exclusively in the west but particularly there-shall be permitted without submitting each separate contract or lease to this parliament for ratification. I take that to be the meaning of the resolution.
Judging from the alacrity with which my hon. friend from Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) has switched his allegiance from op-

position to the resolution to support of the amendment, I gather that he thinks there is a decided difference between the amendment and the resolution itself. There may be some distinction between the two, but for my part I can see no difference in principle. Suppose the amendment carries: it will have to be implemented by legislation; the government will have to bring down amendments not only to the Dominion Lands Act but to the Water-Powers Act and possibly half a dozen others. How can be justify segregating water-powers and deciding that they shall be dealt with in the particular manner provided by the amendment to the resolution, leaving all other resources to be administered as they have been for the last half century or more? No government could justify making that distinction and legislating thereon. It is true, resources are of varying importance and different in character; but there is no difference in principle between the resolution and the amendment, so far as I can see.
We have heard the expression, " no strings on our resources." I wonder whether the acting leader of the opposition desires to have this kind of string, of which he is speaking, tied to the resources of Manitoba after they are transferred. Surely not. No such string is tied to any other province. Well, if it is not desirable to have it tied to the resources when handed over, why is it desirable to have it tied to this particular resource? There must be some reason for it. This is the law and the practice that has obtained for the last half century, and there has been no complaint against it that I have heard. The onus of proving the advisability of a change lies with those who ask for the change. Who wants to make a change in a law of this nature, especially with respect to the Water-Powers Act, which has been in force for so long a time and has been satisfactory to the public interest generally? I have listened attentively to this debate and have read in my spare moments some of the addresses that have been delivered, and I cannot find a valid reason for any change. I find, on the other hand, many reasons, which must appear sensible to thinking men, why we should continue an act that has given satisfaction all round. But no attempt has been made to give any valid reasons for the change. I am prepared to show that no such change should be made, for the simple reason that it would retard the development of resources indefinitely.
Referring to the statement made by my hon.
friend from East Toronto (Mr. Ryck-

Natural Resources-Mr. Motherwell
man), the hon. member criticizes the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), trying to find a statement of his in which he intimates that before any natural resources should be completely returned the matter should be confirmed and ratified and a bill passed through this house. Of course, that is taken for granted. But there is no comparison between that statement and the point under discussion. That deals with all resources; it deals with all three provinces. A bill did pass this house with respect to the resources of Alberta, and a bill will pass this house with respect to all others before any bargain can be consummated.
Let us go back to the development which has recently taken place in Manitoba-and this has been referred to already. Imagine the delay that would have been experienced in connection with the Hudson Bay mining development scheme if that had had to be referred to this house. As everyone knows, the Whitney people's option expired in the fall of 1927; they had to execute it or the option would have expired. If the law had stated that the matter must first be submitted to the house, they could not have taken up their option and gone ahead with the enterprise, with the result that the key to that great northern development might still have remained unturned; that would have been the situation if that proposition had first to be submitted to this parliament for ratification. Then later on power had to be obtained and a lease secured. There was a difference of opinion as to whether the White Mud falls or the Island falls at Churchill should be used. It was decided in favour of the latter, and that meant that Saskatchewan was concerned as well as Manitoba. As a matter of fact, the province of Saskatchewan was consulted with regard to the Hudson Bay mining development, more familiarly known as the Flin Flon, and the representations of both Manitoba and Saskatchewan were incorporated not only in the mining lease but also in the power lease on the Churchill. Quite recently it has been found, too, that in order to facilitate the development of the falls on the Churchill, before mining operations can actually begin in connection with the Flin Flon or the Hudson Bay scheme, a smaller development is required to provide power, in the absence of coal, which is usually used during the construction of the plant. A considerable amount of power is required, and in lieu of coal a small ten or twelve hundred horse power plant was asked for. Under this resolution, that could not be eranted until the meeting of this parliament, 7S594 -40J
when the issue would have to be decided. The result is that the whole mineral and water development of the western country would be tied up if such a resolution as this passed.
Later on, we anticipate, a further request will be made in Saskatchewan. Explorers and those who are investigating these matters, and miners as well, are even now appearing _at Rotten Stone lake, 200 miles north of Prince Albert. Those of you who read the western papers will see that all roads, if not converging in Prince Albert, are at least developed outward from that centre. Fleets of airplanes and dog trains as well are travelling in all directions into the north land with supplies for those who are investigating the possibilities of mining in that vast territory. Now let us suppose this house prorogues, and the Rotten Stone lake or the Reindeer lake or both desire to secure mining lands with accompanying water-powers; they will have to sit by and wait until the house meets next year and we discuss among ourselves-laymen for the most part-what is entirely an engineering proposition. All that procedure would have to be followed before a decision could be arrived at. I cannot imagine anything more ridiculous; yet that is the string my hon. friends opposite have been talking about. Why, it is a cable that they are tying to the whole problem. 1 think the cat is out of the bag; I do not believe they care three hoots about resources. They know the resources will be transferred soon and they want to get into our band wagon and do some of the shouting and claim some of the credit. That is what this resolution amounts to, with its amendment. The same thing might be said with respect to Alberta. I wonder how my hon. friend from Nelson (Mr. Bird), and my friends from Saskatchewan, can advocate a proposition which will hamper the development of that country's resources-resources which have been lying dormant from time immemorial. Those resources are now on the verge of development and they want a further delay until next year. Evidently they think the time is not ripe for the development of these resources and they want to hamper progress for another year by means of this resolution, with its amendment.

speechtext: Has the Dominion government done anything with Alberta's natural resources without consulting the government of Alberta?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Not that I know of With respect to another province an order ir council has been secured which I will read, il you like. This order in council was passed
628	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Motherwell
under date August 1st last, and section 6 thereof refers to the transfer of natural resources and the agreement arrived at between the two governments, the terms of the agreement being set out. This is the last section:
Pending this transfer, the policy of the government of Canada in the administration of the natural resources of Manitoba to be in accord with the wishes of the government of the province.
Nothing could be more complete or more simple than that, and that clause was embodied in the agreement for the express purpose of showing that if this investigation should be prolonged we were sincere in our desire virtually to give them control of their resources by carrying out their wishes in connection with them. That has been the practice of this government ever since we came into power and now it is confirmed by this order in council so that the people of Manitoba will have no reason to object to the length of time involved in a final settlement, because now their resources are administered exactly as they wish. Surely that is the very essence of provincial rights, as recognized by the Liberal party ever since confederation. With respect to the other two provinces, I happened to be acting Minister of the Interior at the time the Hudson Bay mining lease was granted, and I know there can be quite enough delays even under our present system of administration without this parliament making more. With regard to the resources of Alberta and Saskatchewan, the same method of consultation has been in vogue all these years; sometimes they were not so anxious to exercise that right but that is another story. The fact is that we have consulted them and they virtually have had their resources so far as the method of administration was concerned. This agreement gave the assurance that at the earliest possible date we desired to return the resources fully.
While this may not be particularly germane to the question, in passing I would point out that the reason the resources have not been returned by any government is because the original bargains with the provinces were so good that the provinces were not going to have them abrogated until they were given better bargains. Take the province of Saskatchewan; the bargain they made in 1905 proved to be so good that they decided to keep it until some one produced a better bargain. They are awaiting that day yet, and when it comes it will be found that there will be no difficulty in consummating the transaction.

There is another development taking place on Ghost river; that is a bad name, but I understand the river is actually there. We have heard of the Spray falls development up near Banff, and I understand the Ghost river development is midway between Spray falls and Calgary. If we had to wait and go through all this rigmarole and discussion, where would that development be? This is an example of what would happen; this shows how much we know of the engineering features connected with these developments, particularly those members who have not yet visited western Canada. Nothing would be done, and whoever was financing a development never would know where they stood until finally the agreement was passed by this parliament. I hope we will never have such a condition of affairs. Imagine financiers waiting for something to go through this house, say during the first five years we were in office, wondering what was going to happen. You could not get money under those circumstances, and consequently the development of the country, which has been delayed long enough, would be held back still further. While I was listening to my hon. friend who preceded me (Mr. Ryckman) I was going to remark that his province was enjoying its own natural resources but apparently he is desirous of strangling our development while camouflaging and humbugging and pretending he is lying awake nights wondering how to help us.
I do not like to introduce any extraneous matter into this debate, but I am constrained to refer to the Dominion Water Powers Act, passed in 1919, when I think my hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition was a member of the government in power at that time. It is claimed that this act is one of the best ever placed on our statutes as far as the safeguarding of the public interest is concerned, and I would point out that in his present stand my hon. friend the acting leader of the opposition is stultifying himself. The lease was given under this act, which he himself helped to frame.
In connection with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), who moved this resolution, may I say that under this act the government is given power to administer those resources, under conditions more favourable to labour than are contained in any other similar act on this continent. In section 83a of the regulations based on this act we find the following:
Every license shall be deemed to be executed on the express condition that the licensee shall pay or require to be paid to those employed in the construction, alteration, extension, maintenance and operation of the works authorized by such license, wages not less than those

Nalural Resources-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
generally accepted as current for similar services in similar undertakings in the locality, and that such licensee shall maintain conditions of labour not less favourable than those prevailing in similar undertakings in the locality.
That is part of the regulations associated with and based upon this act, and this is the act upon which the lease was based. So our labour men, both in and out of this house, should be the last to argue against the merits of this lease, although I believe my hon. friend intimated that he was not discussing the merits, and I presume this is one of the good things he had in mind.
I shall not dwell further on this matter, Mr. Speaker, except to say that I know hon. gentlemen opposite are hard up for something to talk about this session; they have been looking for a toe-hold ever since this session opened, and so far they have not located one. Lari; year they thought they had something on the Department of Immigration, but that fizzled out. An investigation was made covering weeks and months; they were going to do all sorts of things, but nothing happened. We have had other investigations during the last few years, but they have always back-fired upon hon. gentlemen opposite, and if I know anything about it this will do the same thing. It is not necessary to intimate that they are not going to be much better off when they begin discussing the budget; certainly they will have to get out their magnifying glasses in order to find any fault. They want to find something to object to, on the principle that it is not good politics to agree with everything the government bring down. They are hoping, as was intimated by the hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Ryckman) that something may develop from the situation in Manitoba which will in some way incriminate this government. They do not care anything about the natural resources; if we allow them to do so they will tie them up tighter than you could tie them with a logging chain. They do not care anything about the resources so long as they can make a little capital out of them, and God knows they need it.

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage I
think I should make some further explanation of the contract in connection with the Seven Sisters falls. The question of the desirability of adopting the resolution and amendment has been pretty well discussed, I think, and I have nothing to add except that so far as any safeguards which can be thrown around any department are concerned, I do not think any minister will object to them. I think no one in this 'house has a greater appreciation of the
responsible position occupied by the Minister of the Interior than I have, and whether this resolution is accepted or defeated the one thing I must keep in mind is that in connection with all the leases, of which there are thousands annually, they are apt to be revised and are all subject to consideration by any member of this house who cares to investigate or ask about them. To a very large degree parliament does exercise control over the department which I have the honour to administer. I was especially careful with respect to this particular agreement which is under discussion. There was a great deal of controversy in connection with it, and I may say that since I have been minister there has never been a lease of any moment issued in the province of Manitoba on which there has not been a wide-difference of opinion. This lease presented some very serious difficulties-I mentioned a number of them the other day, and I will not cover that ground again. The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) mentioned one of the most difficult points, namely, that as early as 1893 the Winnipeg Electric Company had started a small development on the Winnipeg river. In 1911 that agreement was amended and brought somewhat under the control of the Department of the Interior, although we did not control the cost of construction or the rentals. That agreement gave the Winnipeg Electric Company the right to divert 9,000 cubic feet from the Pinawa channel in perpetuity for S100 per year. The city of Winnipeg had a similar agreement for a larger amount of water, and they still enjoy that privilege.
May I say here that my sympathy goes out to public ownership and I am willing at every stage to see that there is first a refusal of any utility, be it water-power or anything elset on the part of the representatives of the public. That was the case with respect to this matter. In 1906 the Winnipeg Electric Company had secured all the land around the Seven Sisters development. Hon. members have criticized me somewhat severely with respect to this very matter, but I had nothing to do with the acquiring of that property. From looking over the correspondence complained of, I would assume they were simply taking the precaution that in the event of their developing, or the development by the Manitoba government, they would be protected; for at that time the application of the Manitoba government had priority.
I have given my unqualified backing to the engineers in my department with a view to accomplishing the maximum development on the Winnipeg river stretch, as well as on the
630	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
English river stretch in Ontario, although we have nothing to do with any action taken ' by the Ontario government in that respect. Members of the house will remember the controversy over the Norman dam between the Backus interests and the Dominion and Ontario governments. We have a storage basin in the lake of the Woods that is of inestimable value to the people of the Winnipeg district and the province of Manitoba. Not only that, but we have succeeded in obtaining a storage in lac Seul through the consent of the Ontario government. I will tell my Ontario friends quite frankly that I agreed to the construction of the dam to increase the storage facilities at lac Seul on a cost plus basis, without tender being offered, as I had the utmost confidence in the people who are doing that construction work at lac Seul. This work is being carried on under the auspices of the engineers of the Ontario hydro, and we are putting $500,000 into that enterprise. I still have some confidence in my fellow men and I do not share the suspicion that has been expressed so frequently by those-and I say this with all due deference-who knew very little about the matter they were talking about.
I am not quarrelling about public ownership or private ownership. As I have stated, I first ascertain whether the representatives of the public in any particular locality are desirous of an enterprise being developed under public ownership. Having ascertained to my satisfaction that they do not wish to do this I am prepared to make, with a private corporation, the best deal I can in the public interest and that is what was done in this instance.
Through the arrangement we made with the Ontario government, we were able to say to the people of Manitoba that we were going to increase their power possibilities on the Winnipeg river stretch. Through the securing of this storage basin we were able to increase the development by 300,000 horse-power. We have spent $2,000,000, but we will get that back in instalments from the power company after the development takes place. That is what we have accomplished in the interests of the people of Manitoba.
The Manitoba government could have developed this stretch themselves, but there was the difficulty in removing the Pinawa plant. We had discussed this to some extent with the Winnipeg Electric Company and they believed that their lease in perpetuity costing $100 per year was worth $6,000,000 to them. This is a staggering sum, and it looked like a very difficult proposition to get over. When 
Mr. Bracken came into the matter in 1927 he was told of what we had done in Ontario and that if the Pinawa plant could not be scrapped, thus diverting the flowage over the Seven Sisters reef, then the people of Winnipeg would be deprived of 50,000 horse-power. As I said the other night, he was told that if it was found impossible to deal with the Winnipeg Electric, and he desired to have the Seven Sisters site with the loss of the 50,000 horse-power, I would see that he got it. I made that statement the other night, and I make it again.

I made another stipulation to Premier Bracken; that if he decided later on to recommend dealing with the Winnipeg Electric Company, a separate company should be organized. I did not want to be confronted with the financing of the Winnipeg Electric Company; I wanted to know the provisions contained in the contract and' what the work would cost so that it would be a guide with respect to a future purchase or the control of rates-hence, the Northwestern Power Company. For over a year Mr. Bracken w'as negotiating an agreement with the Winnipeg Electric Company. I was interested in bringing about this development through the scrapping of the Pinawa plant in order that we might get rid of that 9,000 cubic feet in perpetuity and thus have 50,000 horse-power additional on the Seven Sisters reach, and $25,000 or more per year in revenue. But if the Bracken government had been desirous of carrying on this development I would have issued a lease to them. That is my position with respect to private or public ownership. He made his agreement, but I am not going into that. We know he got the power he required for twelve dollars or in the neighbourhood of twelve dollars, between eleven and thirteen dollars. He got the company to agree to scrap the Pinawa plant, to construct the Seven Sisters, to give up their right in perpetuity in that water, they to use it for thirty years for $100. At the end of thirty years rentals prevailing for the water-powers on that reach will prevail as regards the 9,000 cubic feet. But they get in addition, from the moment of construction, fifty

Natural Resources-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton)
cents per horse-power for a minimum rental of 50,000 horse-power or $25,000 a year for the thirty years.
I said that it was a good agreement and I say so still. I did not sign or execute that agreement until I was satisfied that every public interest, so far as I could conceive it, was protected. May I say, with respect to the purchase of the plant, that is provided for at the end of thirty years. If my hon. friends can create in Manitoba a sentiment that can change the Manitoba government or the Manitoba representatives so that they want to buy the plant, every provision and every safeguard are inserted in the agreement to enable them to do so.
The first fifteen years at least from the inception of that power plant will be the worst years, the lean years. People talk very glibly about the way in which private interests get away with all the natural resources of the country. There is not a single natural resource of which I have had the administration since I came into this office that I have sold outright to anyone. They are all under lease and the leases can all be cancelled. I am under review and the operation of my department is under review by the members of the house. If I were sitting in the opposition as a private member and if I had an objection to take to any particular deal consummated in my province or constituency,
I think I could promise you I would bring it to the attention of the house, and I do not think private members are lax in taking an opportunity to complain if they believe they have a right to do so. That is the control parliament exercises over the minister, the department and the government. That is the situation with respect to the Seven Sisters deal. I say most emphatically that no public interest has been neglected with regard to the arrangement.
Let me deal now with the statement of my hon. friend that I have not played fair with the Manitoba members. In the first place, may I refer again to the famous statement that is quoted so often, that was made to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) in the house? After a considerable discussion with reference to the Seven Sisters I made this statement and I want to read the concluding paragraph:
Possibly I have carried that principle too
far-
That is the principle of consulting.

As I say, there may have been misunderstanding, and it is a very critical situation in which to make a mistake .
I did say that, and if it is any satisfaction to my hon. friend, I will say that I did not see him on any of the occasions on which I consulted with the Manitoba members. While I assume my responsibility to every member of this house, I have a particular responsibility to the members who sit on this side of the house, who think as I do, and whose advice I must first seek. I do not desire to evade the advice of any man, but I have a particular responsibility to the members on this side of the house who support the government, and they certainly were consulted.
With respect to leaving it to the legislature,
I suggested that very course to Premier Bracken in July, and I find in the correspondence which was brought down and laid on the table of this house a statement from Premier Bracken citing the statements made by members of the provincial legislature as evidence that the legislature was behind this matter, but he distinctly said that he was going to-take the responsibility- I repeat, I am seeking to evade no responsibility-even to the extent of passing an order in council, which order in council was read by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell).'
