subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to take up but a very short time this afternoon in support of the amendment. Many of us in the house felt that when the resolution of the hon. mem-

Natural Resources-Mr. McRae
ber for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) was unanimously adopted by the house on the 18th of last month, this question of the natural resources of the provinces had been pretty well settled. The speech, however, of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on Thursday evening, followed by this debate, would lead one to believe that our western provinces are yet a long way from getting their resources.
Reviewing tersely that part of the debate, we find that Manitoba had practically consummated its agreement with the government, that Alberta was also in agreement, and that the province of Saskatchewan is now negotiating its case. It would seem that the government might implement the wishes of this house and give early effect to that settlement which we all desire.
The right hon. the Prime Minister spoke the other evening about dividing east and west over this amendment. I have only this comment to make: the great prairie provinces, it would appear, have been very patient and forbearing, and their breaking with the east will depend on how long the government is going to take to give them control of their resources. Parliament has decided the issue, and it seems to me that the matter rests with the government. While I am not familiar with the technicalities of parliamentary procedure, I am quite sure that if this matter was dealt with on a business basis, a final settlement, which is largely a matter of accounting, could be arrived at with very little loss of time.
There are one or two points which have not been considered in this debate to which I would like to draw the attention of hon. members. Eliminating the question of the resources of the western provinces, it would appear that this amendment involves the matter of navigation in our navigable rivers, and the administration of water-powers beyond the boundaries of our provinces. Few, I think, will disagree with the need for protecting the national interests so far as navigation is concerned, and no body is so competent to pass on the national interest as this parliament. I noticed in the Ottawa Citizen this morning a statement that the government proposed to make an announcement on the Beauharnois project some time to-day. It would be very interesting to the members of this house, Mr. Speaker, and very pertinent to this debate, if that statement were before us now. I am not all familiar with the Beauharnois power project, but I am to some extent familiar with the St. Lawrence development, which has been before this government and the country for several years now, and on
which we have expended a large sum of money for the purpose of making an investigation and bringing in a report. If the Beauharnois development does not interfere in any way with the St. Lawrence development, in connection with which our government has already advanced to a final stage, if it does not involve the diversion of the water dealt with and included in the report of the engineers on the St. Lawrence development, then I do not see that nationally we are concerned about it. But on the other hand, if it does not make for the economic development of the entire project as submitted by the engineers, then I think this government and this parliament is vitally concerned in the matter, and we should have before us in considering this resolution the information which it is stated in the press will soon be submitted to the house.
With regard to the water-powers beyond the boundaries of our provinces, there I approach a matter that I know something about. Few of us can appreciate the magnitude of our water-powers beyond our provincial boundaries in our great north country. To get a correct appreciation of their magnitude, you have to go down some of these gigantic rivers and see the numerous falls and rapids that you have to pass as you go along. It is evident that in our estimates of power in our great north, only the big and cheaply developed powers are taken into account. In almost every case there are innumerable sites where smaller developments would have already taken place had those sites been close to centres of population. I think it is a safe statement to make-it is difficult to contradict, at any rate-that the power in our northern country beyond the boundaries of our present provinces is at least twice our present estimates. Those powers cannot be developed to-day on account of the cost and the loss in transmission. There is a demand for the power, but it is too far away for commercial development. But viewing the great advances in electrical science in the past twenty years, particularly in the last ten years, with the marvelous development of radio, who is to say that we are not approaching the time when this power will be available for use in our present centres of population, and perhaps even further afield? I have in mind a statement made last spring by Mr. Isaacs of the British Marconi Company. He stated that his company was experimenting with the transmission of electric power through the ether, and he had sanguine hopes of success crowning their work, in which case the electric power generated on the North American continent
634	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. McRae
would be available for Great Britain. That may seem rather farfetched, Mr. Speaker, but wo do know that during the past few years experimenters in the United States have succeeded in transmitting power for a few hundred feet without the use of a connecting wire. I have no hesitation in saying that I am firmly convinced, as are many men much better qualified to pass an opinion, that by a beam system or some other means, probably a cheap lead wire, not only will the cost of transmission be greatly reduced, but also the loss in transmission will be largely eliminated.
That leads me, Mr. Speaker, to a calculation of the national revenue that would result from the development of these great powers with which a generous Providence has endowed us. Owned and operated by the government for the benefit of the people, I believe the resultant revenue would soon offset, if not wipe out, the debts of our provinces and the national debt as well. I am not enthusiastic about public ownership, I never have been. I have always felt that employing of large staffs as well as competition with private business was not a desirable government activity. But it does seem to me in view of the probable electrical developments that lie ahead that public ownership in the operation and control of our water-powers might well be entertained. To-day we build bridges; no one is needed to look after these structures. Only one or two men would be required to look after a big power development. Thus the objection of a large personnel is now obviated so far as the public ownership of our water-powers is concerned.
Several advantages would follow the government construction of power dams. In the first place, there would be cheap money and cheap credit; in the second place, there would be no promoters' profits, the plant would be developed at cost, and in that way the power would reach the consumer on an actual cost basis. Therefore I believe the time has come when this country should reserve for the benefit of the people all the water-powers not already alienated, to be developed by the government when and as required for the benefit of the nation generally. I would not have the government engage in the retailing of the power thus generated; according to my plan it should sell the power en bloc to distributors as well as to large users of power. In this way the government would always be in a position to see that the charges to the consumer were fair and reasonable.
If any warning is required as to the danger we run in connection with the private develop-
[Mr. McRae.}
ment of electricity in this country, we do not need to look very far afield. I say, and I say it advisedly, Mr. Speaker, that the exploitation of water-powers in the United States is the crime of the century. The best people there realize it, and the information I am about to give hon. members is furnished me by men who are so wrought up over conditions in their own country that they have impressed on me, as they would impress on every member of parliament, the vital importance of preventing similar raids on our own water-powers. Why, I know of one little development of a few thousand horse-power that has changed hands five times in as many years, and to-day the securities representing the entire cost belong to whom? To those who own that water-power. But that is not all. One man in New York by the exploitation of water-powers in the United States cleaned up in 1927 the huge profit of one hundred million dollars. He has given no useful service whatever to his fellow-citizens by that sort of exploitation.
I hope the house will bear with me for a moment while I refer to one state of the union that has prevented similar raids on the public domain. California fortunately has a law on its statute books regulating the development of water-powers. That law has not been detrimental to the development of hydro-electric power within the state. I am told by reputable residents of California that private corporations have developed ample power to meet all requirements; but there has been no exploitation, simply because under that law the expenditure on power developments is supervised and the earnings are regulated.

I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I have fallen so far short in my attempt to lay before the house the great intrinsic values of the water-powers of the Dominion, water-powers which will flow forever, and which will steadily increase in value and in revenue as the years go by. Properly administered, these water-powers will be one of our greatest natural resources, and I for one believe that the time is opportune to surround their development with the restriction provided for by this amendment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it had not been my intention to take part in this discussion, but inasmuch as most of those who have spoken have addressed themselves to the circumstances surrounding the granting of the lease of the Seven Sisters falls water-power site, I feel it incumbent to state to the house the part that I played in the transaction. I do not propose to discuss the lease between the Manitoba government and the Winnipeg Electric Railway Company or any subsidiary company; I consider that is a matter for discussion in the Manitoba legislature and not in this house. But if such is the case it might be interesting to find the reason why the members representing Manitoba in the federal house took a stand on this question at all. To do that it would be necessary to go back to a news item appearing in the Winnipeg papers in 1927, which stated that owing to a report from the city of Winnipeg, that the street railway company of that city had applied to the federal government for a lease of the Seven Sisters falls, the then leader of that government, Mr. Bracken, had stated that he was unalterably opposed to the street railway company getting that permit and was prepared to go, if necessary, as far as expropriating the Pinawa plant of the company on behalf of the province. When that news item reached Ottawa it was a matter of discussion among the Manitoba members, and in order to get behind the Manitoba government on the question a letter was drafted and sent to the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), on February 8, 1928. This letter reads:
That we, the undersigned members of parliament for the province of Manitoba, respectfully request that the power site on the Winnipeg river known as the Seven Sisters falls be retained for the use of the government of the province of Manitoba in their own provincial hydro-electric system.
That was signed by the following members from Manitoba: Bissett, Bancroft, Steedsman, Milne, Ward, Lovie, Beaubien, Glen, Bird, Brown, McPherson, Howden, Thorson, Mc-Diarmid, Woodsworth and Heaps. In other words, sixteen out of the seventeen members representing Manitoba signed this letter which was sent to the Minister of the Interior on February 8, 1928. Subsequently it was found that the government of Manitoba had changed their mind in respect to the development of this power; for after an investigation they had apparently come to the conclusion that it was not wise for the province as a province to develop this water-power. But the one
thing I wish to point out here is that the legislative assembly of Manitoba had passed in 1927 a resolution reading:
Therefore be it resolved that in the opinion of this house-
That is, the Manitoba legislature.
-the government should press for the immediate granting by the federal government all rights to the Seven Sisters falls, situate on the Winnipeg river, said site to be held by the government on behalf of the province of Manitoba.
At the same time the city of Winnipeg passed a resolution protesting against the granting of a lease of the Seven Sisters falls power site on the Winnipeg river to the Backus-Seaman interest, the action of the committee in sending the city solicitor to Ottawa "to be approved and endorsed." The Manitoba members, as has been said by several speakers in this debate, had a good many discussions with the Minister of the Interior relative to this lease and finally, on May 15, 1928, wrote to the federal minister the following letter which was signed, not by all the Manitoba members but by the majority of them. I wish to discuss this letter somewhat in detail. It reads:
The federal members, representing the province of Manitoba, have had before them the question of the disposal of the power of the Winnipeg river at Seven Sisters falls for some time, and after thoroughly going into the matter, beg to advise that their recommendation in connection with same is as follows:
1.	That the site be not disposed of but that the matter be held in abeyance until the close of the next session of the provincial legislature for the purpose of giving the legislature of the province of Manitoba an opportunity to express its opinion in connection with the disposal of the said site or the development of it by the province of Manitoba.
Now the whole" object of the Manitoba members in writing this clause into their letter was based on the fact that the Manitoba legislature-and the legislature, we are given to understand, is supreme-had by formal resolution requested that this particular power site, which was specified in the resolution, be held by and on behalf of the province of Manitoba. Clause 2 of the letter read:
2.	That the said - interval would afford the city of Winnipeg an opportunity to take a referendum vote on the question as to whether the said city desires to develop the power at said site in connection with their present hydro electric system.
That section of the letter was put in as a result of the resolution which I have quoted as having been passed by the city council of Winnipeg, which resolution protested

Natural Resources-Mr. Bissett
against the Seven Sisters power site being handed over to private enterprise. The letter also requested:
That in the event of the province of Manitoba deciding to develop the said power as a provincial undertaking, that they be given said right upon request.
And further, that if neither the province of Manitoba nor the city of Winnipeg wish to develop the said site, the present applicant, the Winnipeg Electric Railway Company, be given priority to any other private corporation to develop same, subject to the usual restrictions imposed by the water-power regulations.
Now I contend that that letter presented a very fair view on behalf of the Manitoba members. We insisted that inasmuch as the legislature of the province had asked that this site be held for the province, in our opinion this should be done; and we also asked that, inasmuch as the city of Winnipeg had protested against the alienation of this power to private interests, if the province was not interested the city of Winnipeg should be given the next opportunity to develop the site; and, thirdly, that failing either of these parties becoming interested, the railway company, the present applicant, should be considered ahead of any other applicants subsequently applying.
As the house has been told by a number of speakers, various interviews took place between the Minister of the Interior and the members from Manitoba, and I wish it distinctly understood that the Manitoba members were not all of one opinion regarding this proposition. The minister has been quoted with reference to a promise he gave the Manitoba members prior to prorogation, and which has been the subject of a great many remarks, not all of them to his credit. I feel that I should explain exactly what my position wa. with respect to the promise made by the minister. When the house prorogued I was under the impression that before anything further was done in regard to this power site I would be consulted, and I want the house to understand that prior to the conference and agreement being signed between the provincial and federal governments with respect to the natural resources I had not changed my mind in regard to this deal between the street railway company and the provincial government. Further I want to say that until the agreement was made between the province and the Dominion with reference to the transfer of the natural resources I did not at any time sec the minister or have any discussion with him by letter or otherwise in regard to the matter.

However, I must say that I saw the minister in Winnipeg, after the agreement was signed, and with a number of other members discussed the whole agreement with him. On that occasion I told the minister that since there was an agreement in existence between the province of Manitoba and the federal government with respect to 'the disposition of the natural resources, my position was that the federal government should stand by that agreement. I want this distinctly understood:	Had I been able to express myself
prior to the drawing up of this agreement I would have objected to the insertion of clause 6; however, I did not have the opportunity of doing so and rather than see the agreement jeopardized by any controversy, which certainly would not have any effect on a binding agreement of that kind, I withdrew any opposition I had to the Seven Sisters deal, because it was bound up with the general natural resources agreement.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I had just stated that at the time of my last interview with the Minister of the Interior the agreement between the province of Manitoba and the Dominion government relative to the transfer of the natural resources had been concluded. Consequently, I found I was in the position of having either to oppose the whole natural resources agreement or to accept it in toto, and inasmuch as the Seven Sisters power site was part of that agreement I was forced to withdraw any opposition I might have had to the Seven Sisters falls project going ahead. I contended then and I still contend that the Manitoba members should have been consulted prior to the inclusion of clause 6 in that agreement, but after considering the difficulty which has been encountered during the years since this natural resources agreement has been the subject of controversy within the province and within this house, I felt that I must not do anything which would in any way defeat that objective.
The resolution on the order paper reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, no disposition of the natural resources,-
Or the water-powers, as the amended resolution reads.
-under the control of the federal government, shall be effective until ratified by parliament.

Natural Resources-Mr. Heaps
I do not propose to vote for this resolution.
I contend, rightly or wrongly, that the disposition of the natural resources in any of the provinces is not a matter for parliament, but is a matter for the legislatures of the provinces concerned. If the province of Manitoba had had full control of its natural resources this question of the Seven Sisters power site would never have arisen in this house, and, therefore, I urge again the necessity of turning over the natural resources of each of the provinces to their respective owners with as little delay as possible. I do not think it is fair for the members for Manitoba to try to interfere in any way with the natural resources belonging to the provinces of Saskatchewan or Alberta. We have it on the word of the Prime Minister that agreements along the lines of the Manitoba agreement have been effected with the other provinces, so I do not think there is any necessity for this resolution.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I opposed and still oppose the alienation of the Seven Sisters power site in the public domain of the province of Manitoba and I regret that this very valuable power site is lost to the public ownership interests in that province. As I stated at the beginning of my remarks, the responsibility for this power site being handed over to private interests is a matter which rests entirely with the legislators of the province of Manitoba, and any criticisms I have to make will be made as a private citizen of that province and not as a member of this house.

I intend, Mr. Speaker, to vote for the amendment. Not because it happens to be moved by a member of the Conservative party; I would have'voted for it had it come from any other section of the house. One of the first things I did this session was to ask the right hon. Prime Minister, in connection with the St. Lawrence development, whether the house would be given an opportunity to discuss the question. I am in favour of all these important questions being dealt with by parliament, not by order in council. I believe that is good Liberal doctrine. I know it is characteristic for the Conservative party to become Liberal when in opposition, and for the Liberal party to become Conservative when in power. Evidently we are witnessing such a phenomenon at the present time on the question of orders in council. I remember very well that one of the very last speeches by the grand old chieftain of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was delivered in the city of Ottawa in January of 1019, and it was a scathing denunciation of government by order in council. I oppose government by order in council, whether it has to do with the Beauhamois scheme or with the Seven Sisters scheme. If the province of Manitoba were in full possession of their natural resources, I could have no objection whatsoever to any disposition that the provincial government might make of this particular power site. But the Manitoba government did not have that power last year when they requested the Dominion government to hand over the Seven Sisters power site to the Winnipeg Electric Company. If this resolution we are now considering had been in effect a year ago, then I believe we should all have been better off for it; and the fact that it would have been a good thing a year ago is no argument that it is not a good thing to-day. It merely indicates that we are somewhat late in having a motion of this character discussed by the house. The resolution is not aimed at Saskatchewan or Alberta or any of the other provinces. I believe that if this resolution were adopted by this house such questions as the Beau-harnois development on the St. Lawrence would also of necessity have to come to the house for ratification. When a power development is under consideration, covering a lease of fifty years or probably longer, then a delay of three or four months is of little consequence to the people of the Dominion. Moreover, these private corporations who intend to develop these natural resources are not undertaking their development from philanthropic motives; they are developing them because they believe it will be profitable. I am sure, therefore, that these financial corporations could very well afford to wait a few months until parliament could ratify an agreement. Consequently I am in favour of the amendment, which has now been restricted to water-powers. The case of Alberta has been cited by my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Adshead). I want to assure him that there is no analogy between Alberta and Manitoba; the two cases are entirely different. subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
My hon. friend has made two speeches on this subject already, and I propose to take up only ten or fifteen minutes of the time of the house. I do not wish to make any insinuations about my hon. friend's motives in moving this resolution; I believe him to be quite sincere, but I do think he displayed bad judgment in the drafting of the resolution. I will not say of him unkind things such as he has said of the Minister of the Interior, but I have some knowledge of the difficulties with which the minister has to deal in connection with these matters of leases and so on, and I know that no man who has

Natural Resources-Mr. Dunning
occupied that position has guarded the public interest more meticulously than lias the present Minister of the Interior.
Then let us pass on from the water in the Winnipeg river; let us consider the prospector who is in the Rocky mountains looking for a ledge of gold or some other precious or base metal. When he found that ledge, if my hon. friend's system were in vogue he would have to worry about which side of the divide he was on, and sometimes in the Rocky mountains it is rather difficult to tell which side of the divide you are on. If he were on the British Columbia side he could go to the office of the nearest mining recorder and there and then get possession of his claim subject to the laws of the province, but if my hon. friend's system were in operation and his find happened to be on the Alberta side of the divide, an act of this parliament confirmed by the senate would be necessary before that prospector could do anything. Surely that is an absurd situation. As I say, this parliament has taken fifty years to build up a body of law which will ensure that successive ministers will administer these resources in the best interests of the people of the country. Parliament is made acquainted each year, through documents tabled here, with the manner in which the minister for the time being has been discharging his stewardship, and of the hundreds and thousands of dispositions which have taken place and which have been reported to this house, the only one to be discussed during the course of this debate is that in connection with the Seven Sisters falls.
Now may I refer to the policy of taking advice from the provincial governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta with respect to the disposition of their important resources. I want to say that ever since the present government came into office in 1921 the Minister of the Interior has consistently followed the policy of consulting the western governments with respect to the disposition of major resources of this character. He consistently consulted me during the time I was premier of my province; I know he has consistently consulted the premier of Alberta and the premier of Manitoba as well during that period. Is that policy wrong? It is an acknowledgment of what we were debating in this house the other day; it is an acknowledgment that with respect to these resources in these three prairie provinces the Dominion is in reality a trustee. These provinces have had responsible government for nearly twenty-five years. Who then should speak for the people of these provinces if not
the responsible governments elected by the people? How can this government expect to secure information with respect to what the people of a province require if not from the government of that province? What would be said if we refused to regard a statement made by the government of Ontario or the government of Quebec, as expressing the wili of the people of these provinces? One has only to imagine it.

We would not put up with
it.

speechtext:
That is what we would
have to put up with in the west if the sort of thing advocated by the resolution and the amendment were permitted.
I listened with a great deal of interest and pleasure to the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. McRae); I was very much interested in what he said in respect to waterpower and the desirability of public control- and I use those words "public control" advisedly, because that does not always involve public development even in the public-ownership province of Ontario. However, I suggest that my hon. friend was preaching to the wrong congregation this afternoon. When be spoke, and spoke truly, of the situation which has developed in the United States he did not answer his own obvious question, "Why has it developed?" It has developed because in the United States, as in Canada, there is a federal system of government and the states do control their own water-power. He cited one instance which proved that point, when he referred to the very excellent laws on the statute books of the State of California for the control of water-powers within that state. Yes, that is true; the laws are on the Statute books of the state of California, and not on those of the congress of the United States. His arguments were splendid, but they were addressed to the wrong body.
However, I agree that his argument would apply with respect to the Northwest territories lying north of our existing provinces; I think my hon. friend made reference to the Northwest territories and the wonderful water-powers on the northern rivers. It seems a strange thing that after starting to deal with all the resources of the country the discussion finally narrows down to water-powers, and then practically altogether to the water-power of the middle west. My hon. friend even left those alone; he was inclined to concede that with respect to the resources of the western provinces the governments of those provinces should be considered, and then he went away

Natural Resources-Mr. Dunning
off to the north of the existing boundaries of our western provinces, although I venture to say that not a single water-power has been alienated in that region as yet, because no one wants them. I agree that it is well for this parliament and for all the provincial legislatures having these matters within their control to bear in mind what my hon. friend said with regard to the necessity of conserving these great resources for the maximum benefit to the public to whom they belong, but again it is a question of whose jurisdiction obtains. If this parliament or any member of it set up .a claim to-day to the water-powers of the province of Quebec or those of the province of Ontario I can just see my hon. friends opposite rising in their serried ranks to protest against any such claim on the ground of provincial rights. We have often heard that cry in this house, but we in the west possess provincial rights just as much as they are possessed in the older provinces of Ontario and Quebec.

that direction, and this government has made greater progress in that way than any othct government since the provinces were formed, and we intend to continue along that. line. That is the reason for all the criticism, and that government is not regarded as a supporter of this government politically; it is a Progressive government.

There can be no question in the mind of anyone that the minister acted in accordance ' with the desires of the government of Manitoba, a government which must be presumed a responsible government, responsible to the legislature of that province. Let me apply the principle to the province of Alberta. Would anyone in this house say that if the government of Alberta were consulted, as is frequently the case, by the Minister of the Interior with respect to the disposition of
[Mr. Dunninir.J

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
If the hon. member is
correct, then the Minister of the Interior is to get it coming and going; he is to be wrong if he does consult with the provincial government and take their view's, and he is to be wrong if he does not consult with them. Applying the principle of public ownership to the province which is the best known throughout the world for public ownership development of electrical power-the province of Ontario-I believe I am correct in saying that power sites are disposed of to private interests; not all the power sites in the province of Ontario are held for ever until they can be incorporated in the provincially owned power system. I do not blame the province of Ontario for doing this; they are dealing with a condition and not a theory. There are areas in the northern part of that province similar to the northern parts of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta where great developments are in prospect; where for many years there can be but one user of the electrical powers created. I do not blame the Ontario government for saying in such cases, " You can have this power to develop, but it must be developed under certain terms." That is precisely what is happening in the northern parts of Manitoba and Saskatchewan; I do not know so much about Alberta.
If any such amendment as this passed the house, carrying with it as it would the necessity of amending the law, it would tend to strangle, as nothing else could, the industrial development of the resources of northern Manitoba and northern Saskatchewan. Why is that? In certain parts of this country it is possible to get coal for the purpose of developing the large base metal resources, but in these northern parts it is necessary on economic grounds to use electricity, and that electricity can only be secured from one source, the streams and falls which are there. Shall we refuse to allow that development to go on? Shall we say to everyone, "You must take the chance of running the gauntlet of parliament"? This house could do nothing which would be more sure of stifling and

Natural Resources-Mr. Geary
strangling the industrial development of the northern parts of those western provinces than to pass this resolution or the amendment and to amend the laws which would be necessary to be amended if the resolution or the amendment were passed. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, which are satisfactory to me, I intend to vote against both the resolution and the amendment.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be assumed from the speeches of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) that water-powers as distinguished from other natural resources have some special attributes and characteristics. That being the case, it follows naturally that they are deserving of some special treatment, and this amendment, as I read it, provides that special treatment. The resolution, as amended, reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, no disposition, of the water-powers, under the control of the federal government, shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
I understood the Prime Minister to say the other day that we would be breaking an agreement by the passing of this amendment -referring, I take it, to the agreement made with the province of Manitoba in July of last year. With all due respect, Mr. Speaker,
I cannot see how that could be. If that agreement entered into under an order in council in July last is a binding agreement as to resources under the control of the federal government, then this resolution cannot be said to be a breach of that agreement because it deals with the resources now under the control of the federal government. If the resources passed under that agreement from the control of the federal government no action of this house under the resolution could have any effect upon that contract. It has been said that we would be acting in breach of that agreement by discussing the matter in parliament and passing a resolution which refused to ratify the agreement. I say that is precisely what parliament is for, otherwise why do we bring conventions and protocols here for ratification? Simply to have the rubber stamp of parliament's approval put upon them, or to 'have discussions upon them and to ratify them when found proper? The Prime Minister, speaking only a few days ago on the proposed amendment to the Navigable AVaters Protection Act, told the house that there was already a clause in that act which would enable parliament to undo what had been done by order in council or through the granting of a permit under the provisions of that act. In principle that is the sort of thing
we are doing here to-day. AYe are discussing this matter after the thing has been done; whether it should have been done and whether or not it should be ratified. If we have not the power to change it no harm is done; if it requires ratification we are within our rights in refusing ratification. In any case we have the satisfaction of having the whole question disclosed and aired in the house. I think the resolution as it now reads will find ready acceptance by the member for AVinnipeg South Centre (Mr' Thorson), and perhaps by the member for South AVinnipeg (Mr. Mc-Diarmid), who seems to have agreed throughout the negotiations with the member first
named.	.	.
I do not think the member for AVinnipeg South Centre is in the house, but he will recognize the words he used and which are found in Hansard o,f February 28, 1929, on page 559. He was there discussing clause 6 of the agreement entered into with the province of Manitoba in July of last year, and he says, at the bottom of the page:
I have this criticism to make, namely, that the change in policy was so vital tnat it should not have become effective until ratified by parliament. and that a rider should have been attached to clause 6 of the natural resources agreement to the effect that until the fundamental change in the policy of administering the resources had been approved by parliament, the change of policy indicated by clause o should not go into effect.
On the same page, he has the following to say:	_ #
In view of the differences of opinion that existed in this house; in view of the differences of opinion that existed in Manitoba; m view of the undertaking which the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) gave on the floor ot this house, and in view of the developments that have taken place, I think it would have been a wise course to follow to take the view that before this fundamental change in the policy of administering the natural resources of Manitoba should come into effect, it should he ratified by parliament. That would have been in the interests of all concerned here; it would certainly have been in the interests ot the government of Manitoba which finds itself in such difficulties to-day.
I assume that the member for AVinnipeg South Centre, and the members of the house who agree with that hon. gentleman and have agreed with him throughout these negotiations, cannot do otherwise than support the amendment now before the house.
I am not so sure about the member for Marquette (Mr. Glen). There have been occasions when that hon. gentleman has been decidedly of one opinion, but when the time came for a vote he cast his vote the other way, and I believe that is his case to-day. Let me remind the house of what the member for Marquette said when this matter was
64S

Natural Resources-Mr. Geary
under discussion on the 28th of February last. His remarks will be found on page 543 of Hansard and what his concern was throughout the negotiations with the Minister of the Interior is stated as follows:
We were determined to do all in our power to delay the issuance of that lease until the representatives o_f the people of Manitoba had had an opportunity of declaring themselves on the matter in the legislative assembly.
That is good doctrine, and if those hon. gentlemen are disposed to adhere to what they said at that time, the opportunity is still before them to see that this particular transaction and others like it are ratified in the house and come up for discussion and action before the legislative assembly of Manitoba. As regards the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), he can see no good whatever, now or at any previous time, in a member of the house holding views similar to those which have been expressed by my hon. friends from Marquette and Winnipeg South Centre. So in one case I would expect and in the other I would hope that when the yeas and nays are called for on this resolution, my two hon. friends, with those who have been closely associated with them, will be found voting in favour of the amendment now before the house. True, there is this to be said of the hon. member for Marquette, that he found himself at the end of his address able to say that he was supporting his government. He said:
, I believe that the province of Manitoba through its legislature is alone responsible to its citizens for what is done with that power site. Our duty ceased as soon as the agreement was arrived at between the Dominion government and the province.
I Submit to the house for its consideration whether that last clause is inspired by some sort of feeling of relief or of disappointment.
I do not propose to refer at any length to the controversy that has arisen between the Minister of the Interior and certain hon members representing constituencies in Manitoba; but it seems to me strange that the other night-and I regret to say this is the second time I have spoken on this matter-the minister interrupted me when I was speaking, and his interruption was welcomed, to say that when he answered the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) last year, he was referring to a difference of opinion, not between parties in the legislative assembly or parties amongst the citizen body of Winnipeg or of Manitoba, but existing among members from Manitoba m this house. My hon. friend narrowed that a little again to-night. He said that he was quite willing and ready at all times to discuss

matters with members representing constituencies in the particular province affected. He preferred to assuage the anxieties of the members from that particular province who were with him, thought as he did and sat on the same side of the house as he did. If it be a desirable thing that the Minister of the Interior, in discussing the affairs of his department and deciding what he is to do in carrying on those affairs, should consult any body of members of this house, even restricting that body to members of the house who are on the same side as he is then it seems to me a certain principle is admitted, namely, that all the members of the house are entitled to some opportunity for discussion and consideration of the action to be taken in regard to a transaction about to be consummated. Having admitted the principle, I cannot for the life of me see why he will not go the whole distance and say that, if it is proper to consult members from that particular province or even members from that province who sit on the same side of the house as he does, it is proper that he should consult all the members of parliament who are here and prepared to discuss matters of that sort. I think that was in the mind of the Minister of the Interior before, because there is in the file that was laid on the table a letter which shows conclusively that the question of having the legislature of Manitoba consider this particular transaction, the Seven Sisters falls, was before the parties who entered into the contract in August last, since Mr. Bracken writes to the Minister of the Interior as follows on 31st May, 1928. He had apparently been down here discussing the matter of the Seven Sisters falls with the Minister of the Interior. He begins his letter thus:
In view of some of the statements made to us in the conference in Ottawa on Friday last with regard to the provincial legislature dealing the power question, I am transmitting to you for your information. . . . press reports of what different members of the legislature have said.
Therefore I take it that at the conference with the Minister of the Interior it was considered proper by at least some members of the conference that the matter should be considered by the legislature of Manitoba before action was finally taken. That is carrying out precisely the views of my hon. friends from Marquette and Winnipeg South Centre.
There is just one comment I have to make on the famous letter of June 7, and I am not going to refer again to what my hon. friend's action seems to have been, writing so soon after, in fact the next day after he had in-

Natural Resources-Mr. Geary
formed the house, as he did, that there should be no further delay. He says in this letter:
In view of the fact that delay of a month or so will not injure the prospects of this development-
I commend that to the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean). As a matter of fact, the application was then practically one year old and applications for power development of any size-and power developments of any size are the only ones in which we are particularly concerned-do not suffer one bit by waiting over for a session of a legislature or of parliament. Everyone knows there is no enterprise or business undertaking that is so much sought for by certain monied interests as a water-power and its development. As a matter of fact, much higher prices may be realized if there is any delay in granting the lease or the right to develop the power. In any event it cannot be shown in a single instance the any damage would foe done in the case of any individual water-power, especially one of great size or potentiality, if the matter had to rest over. A company having a permit and knowing that it had to obtain the approval of parliament, no harm would be done by its having to wait for that length of time.
As a matter of fact, I doubt if there would be any difficulty as regards financing, because once having secured a permit and no great public question being aroused over the matter, people could go so far as to finance the whole proposition on the assumption that the matter would, being altogether honest, straightforward and aboveboard, be ratified at the next session of the legislature or of parliament.
It may be said at this point that there is no provision in the resolution for securing ratification by the provincial legislature, but that would be a mere quibble. We cannot legislate in regard to the provincial assembly; we can legislate in regard to our own action, and when we say by resolution that no alienation of a water-power shall be given until ratified by this parliament, we are by that very act giving time for the provincial assembly to make up its mind and make its deliberations in the case of that water-power and to communicate the result to parliament. I venture to say, that being done, there would never be the slightest suggestion that it would not be sanctioned by parliament after having been passed, by the provincial legislature concerned..
There is one feature to which I .must refer in connection with the meeting at which this agreement was so hurriedly come to. This was on July 3. The matter about which most
discussion arose, about which there was most concern, was what? Natural resources. The natural resources in the House of Commons are under the charge of the Minister of the Interior, and yet that meeting of representatives of the Dominion government and of the government of Manitoba met without the one man present who had the most to do with the whole transaction, and within whose knowledge it was whether or not the natural resources could be disposed of advantageously in any manner that might be suggested.
He did not know anything about it; he did not hear about it until after the whole thing had been done. Is it any wonder that my friends from Manitoba were slightly shocked to hear of the rapidity with which that particular transaction went through? Even after the door was locked, after that particular horse was stolen, they still had the consolation of meeting the minister at Winnipeg, at which meeting they made their .protest, not sorry, I should judge in some cases, to find that their protests were alii too late.
When that conference met in July, 1928, the ministers of the crown present knew, or if they did not they ought to have known, that there was great public discussion about the granting of a lease to a private corporation for the development of power at the Seven Sisters falls. That was a very important public matter. It was not a matter that was heard of merely round the comer; it was discussed in all the newspapers and formed the main topic of news and editorial writing for a very considerable time. It was a matter of the highest importance to the people of the city of Winnipeg, and yet it had not been heard of, according to the Prime Minister, it was not made a note of in carrying on the discussions and the negotiations, and it was not mentioned when the final agreement was carried through.
We are not discussing, I take it, so much what will happen in regard to this or that water-power. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) has made his whole attack upon the inconvenience in point of time that would occur because the granting of a lease had to await action by this house. What I take it is the point and the whole point of this discussion is whether or not we have abandoned to the government, to the executive, entirely so that we cannot have it back, the power of dealing with the vast natural resources, not by order in council, but by parliament in free and open discussion. That, it seems to me, is the point at issue here, and not the consideration of any question of mere delay being caused by the adoption of a rule that the

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to direct the attention of the house for a very few minutes to what has been said with regard to the correspondence which passed between the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), the government of Manitoba, and the other parties
in connection with the transaction under discussion. I feel that perhaps the house has not appreciated the effect of the correspondence quoted by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) between the Minister of the Interior and the Premier of Manitoba prior to February, 1928. There seemed to be a disposition on the part of some hon. members to suggest bad faith on the part of my colleague and I was glad to-night to hear the assurance that the criticism was directed simply to the minister's exercise of judgment. But that does not fit in very well with the construction which was sought to be placed on some of the correspondence. A telegram of February 6, 1928, was read which had been sent by my friend the minister intimating that the Winnipeg Electric Company had not made any further request. In order to contradict that statement or to make it appear that it was not true certain letters were quoted, one of August 7, 1927-this was a wrong date; I think the hon. member will find the correct date was August 23, and two others of October 28 and November 18, 1927. The three letters referred to were not in any way contradictory of what had been said by the Minister of the Interior; they simply followed the original application of the Winnipeg Electric Company, the letter of August 23, 1927, gave the name of the company to whom it was desired the license should be given if any was to be issued. The letter of October 2S simply suggested that the status quo be preserved, and that applications for homestead rights had better be reserved. For what? Not for the Winnipeg Electric, but, as the letter itself shows, for the development of water-powers. Exactly the same sort of suggestion appears in the letter of November 18, 1927, in which it is proposed that it would perhaps be as well not to have settlers put improvements on the land, in view of the fact that applications for power leases were outstanding.
Now, what applications were outstanding at that time? Not simply the application of the Winnipeg Electric but the application as well of the province of Manitoba. All these letters amounted to were simply suggestions by one of the applicants that the land be so maintained that water-power leases could be granted if the government so decided. Very different altogether from the suggestion that my hon. friend the minister was in some way or other endeavouring to mislead those with whom he was communicating by stating that the company was not "urging" the lease. What was proposed was, I think, a perfectly proper and logical and natural thing for any applicant to suggest. I will not detain the

Natural Resource-Mr. Ralston
house by quoting the letters in full. I repeat that they refer to water-powers, not to the Seven Sisters falls, and not to the application of any particular company.
Now, let me refer to the other matter which has been dealt with at great length with regard to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior. He made statements to the house on June 6, 1928. I am afraid hon. members have perhaps not appreciated exactly the order in which those statements were made, or their contents. There has been repeatedly quoted a statement by the hon. minister in reply to a question addressed to him by the hon. leader of the opposition, in which he said:
I may assure my hon. friend that until that difference of opinion is settled I am not going to issue any license for that water-power. 1 think I may assure my hon. friend of that.
But that was not the final statement. Following that, as the records shows, was a long speech by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and then the Minister of the Interior replies to him in these words:
I am going to say very frankly here and now that notwithstanding the fact that at present the government have adopted a line of action with respect to the Seven Sisters falls I am not in any particular hurry to come to any decision about that matter, largely because of the fact that the members of this house have expressed very decided opinions about the matter as federal members. I am not very much disturbed by the statement that there must be immediate action; I have investigated the matter pretty well and I think there is plenty of time to give ample consideration to this matter before it is decided. In order to settle the question, and in order to prevent any delay, I do not see any reason why we should not await the action of the city council of Winnipeg and of the provincial government, which must take the responsibility, before a final decision is made here. I think that should satisfy my hon. friend.
Now, that is the understanding arrived at, that my hon. friend would await the action of the city of Winnipeg and the provincial government, and would consult the federal members from the province. My hon. friend from Nelson (Mr. Bird) understood that, as has already been pointed out by the Minister of the Interior this afternoon. The hon. member for Nelson was quite frank in his statement to the house. He said:
_ It may be against my disposition to oast unjustifiable reflections upon the government, or upon the Minister of the Interior, and I do not go as far as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) went. The Minister of the Interior did say to us quite plainly, before we left for home last session, that he could not hold up this matter until the Manitoba legislature met: he was very frank about that. But if I did not misunderstand

him. and there is always the possibility that I might have-I can confirm what I am saying by my own diary, and his words in the house seem to confirm it-he said that before anything was done the members for Manitoba would be consulted.
That is what my hon. friend himself understood. And what does the minister do? I ask hon. members to consider this in all fairness, because some caustic criticism has been made of the Minister of the Interior. The minister waits for over three months, instead of a month or a month and a half; he goes to Winnipeg twice and consults members there. True, he did not consult all the members; I understand that, and the minister has been quite frank about it. But he did consult the majority of the members there, and the whole resources question intervenes; it comes up about a month after the statement was made in the house. A very different situation presents itself to him. The government had arrived at an agreement to transfer the whole of the natural resources to the province of Manitoba subject to certain stipulations, and provided the house ratified it and in the meantime they consented to dealing with its natural resources according to the wishes of Manitoba under the powers which the statutes conferred on the executive. Let me right here refer to what has been said by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary). That hon. gentleman has talked about the alienation of natural resources otherwise than by parliament, I would ask the house to bear this in mind, that we are discussing a power which has been exercised under the Dominion Water Powers Act for a good many years. The governor in council is authorized under that act bo grant licenses. I quite understand that there is no authorization to transfer them absolutely. And that, it seems to me, is the distinction which is to be made in connection with the argument which is being advanced on the other side of the house. There is a difference between administrative action and legislative action. Administrative action is taken every day. The Minister of Public Works, after a vote is passed here, has to do, let us say, with the construction of a building; if something goes wrong there you do not take away the power of the minister to construct that building and confine that power to parliament. You censure him if censure is justified, and you may have him dismiss someone if there is someone in the department who is not acting properly. But that does not give you any justification to come here and say, "We are going to remove from the minister the administrative power and vest it in the

Natural Resources-Mr. Ralston
legislative body." Under the Dominion Water Powers Act the government has to-day-as I know the province of Nova Scotia and the province of British Columbia have, and as I think the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec also have-the right to grant licenses of water-powers; and these licenses are being granted: every day as an executive act. My hon. friend speaks of a change of policy in connection with paragraph 6 of the agreement, which indicated that this government was going to follow the wishes of Manitoba, and he suggests that this ought to have been made a matter of legislation. But the legislation was on, the statute book. This government had the power, under the Water Powers Act, to do all that was d*>ne in this case, namely, to grant the license to the Winnipeg Electric Company or to Manitoba as the case might be. And that was all that this government did. It did not need further administrative power at all; it had it. It needed legislative power if there was to be an absolute transfer of natural resources. Take the province of Nova Scotia, for instance:	every day the Minister of Mines
grants licenses on mineral areas. That is administrative, and such action the government can take. If, on the other hand, he proposes to transfer the whole of the minerals of the province, that is to say, to transfer the absolute fee simple, in that case legislation is required. And such legislation was provided for in the agreement between Manitoba and this government. We must, I say, carefully distinguish between legislative power and the administrative power, the administrative function vested in the Dominion government and in every local government in Canada, and that power it is now proposed to take away from this federal government by the resolution now before the house. We are losing sight of this distinction, and it would contravene the very spirit of the working out of our constitution if we decided to make this legislative body an administrative body.
My hon. friends have been most severe in their criticism, but they do not charge the minister with being dishonest and I do not think they should assume that a government will exercise the powers vested in i.t dishonestly. But it is suggested that because this transaction has taken place-a transaction which is quite within the powers of the executive- the remedy should be to remove entirely the power which is properly vested in those by whom it should be exercised. That is not a logical suggestion; it is not workable; it is not a practical suggestion. I do not think it is a suggestion which will commend itself to the judgment of the house.
Many times the terms monopolies and corporations and trusts and capitalists have been used in the debate, and it seems to me that it is these terms which have influenced at least some hon. members more than anything else in connection with the transaction. If this lease had been made to the government of Manitoba, that would have been all right; but because the licensee happens to be called a "company", with "limited" added thereto, that makes it all wrong. I submit-and I do not think one needs to make very much of an argument about it-that if the transfer to the licensee is made at the request of a public body, in this case the government of Manitoba, the province of Manitoba, the principle of public ownership is just as much respected as if the transfer had been made to the premier of Manitoba, or the Minister of Public Works or the Attorney General.
I do not think there has yet been read the statement with regard to the proposal of this government to transfer this lease to the province of Manitoba. The statement is contained in a letter of August 18, 1928, to Mr. Bracken. It reads:
Dear Mr. Bracken,
After discussing with my colleagues the applications made for the right to develop the Seven Sisters power site on the Winnipeg river, *we have decided to offer the Manitoba government the right to develop this power site. It is to be understood, however, that the lease will be in accordance with the provisions of the Dominion water-power regulations governing the leasing of power sites.
We will prepare an interim license at once if this meets with the approval of your government.
Yours sincerely,
Charles Stewart,
Minister of the Interior.
The federal government is there proposing to transfer, not to the Winnipeg Electric but to the government of Manitoba itself, this power site. And what is the reply? It is contained in a letter from Premier Bracken dated August 21, 1928, addressed to the Hon. Charles Stewart. It reads:
Dear Mr. Stewart,
I have your letter of the 18th instant, in which you advise that after consultation with your colleagues you had decided to offer the government of Manitoba the right to develop Seven Sisters power site, in accordance with the regulations of the Water Powers branch.
I beg most respectfully to point out that no matter how- willing our government might be to accept this offer, it has no legal authority to do so. Might I also point out that the policy of this government under the circumstances now obtaining, as you know, is not to develop this site itself but to permit it to be developed by the company which now controls in perpetuity nearly one half of the water in this section of the Winnipeg river. _ This policy was arrived at after having obtained opinions

Natural Resources-Mr. Ralston
and recommendations from the Dominion Water Powers branch and advice from expert hydroelectric engineers both in your department and outside.
The minister has mentioned two electrical engineers, Doctor Hogg and Mr. Gaby.

speechtext: That might be misunderstood. I merely mentioned Mr. Gaby as an engineer in whom I had complete confidence and who was an associate of Doctor Hogg; but he was not employed on that work.

speechtext:
Then I am corrected as regards Mr. Gaby. The letter proceeds:
In accordance with that policy, the government negotiated a contract with the Winnipeg Electric Company and the North Western Power Company. We were successful in obtaining terms which would make for the complete realization of the plans and policies for which your Water Powers branch has been contending for several years. The contract provides for the abandonment of the Pinawa development and the closing of the channel, and for the single development of the maximum power possibilities of the Winnipeg river at the Seven Sisters site. It also assures the province of an adequate supply of power sufficient to meet the needs of the provincial hydro system and of rural Manitoba for the next thirty years, at a very low price.
By this contract the perpetual right of the company to the Pinawa flow will be extinguished and the acquisition of the Seven Sisters development by the province at the end of thirty years made possible.
We should have preferred undertaking the development ourselves but for the fact that under the circumstances existing it would have been an unsound financial proposition and would have prejudiced the principle of public ownership. The arrangement entered into makes possible immediate development under conditions where rates can be controlled, the interests of the public adequately protected, and the development taken over at the end of thirty years under conditions much more likely to make possible successful operation as a publicly owned enterprise, without our having to expropriate or to pay for the present Pinawa plant or the perpetual rights now held by the company.
These are the reasons why it was not granted to the government of Manitoba direct. But, Mr. Speaker, I contend that the government can be taken prima facie to represent the people of Manitoba. My hon. friend from Vancouver North (Mr. McRae) spoke this afternoon about what had been done in the country to the south, where power developments were kept for the people, as he said. I do not know who better represents the people of a province than the government elected by that province; I believe this provincial government was elected in 1927 and received a vote of confidence in a by-election in 1928. This Manitoba government, by

order in council which I think has been read, definitely requested the government of the Dominion to issue this license to the Winnipeg Electric Company. Let me read just a paragraph:
And whereas the said interim license was prepared by the water powers branch of the Dominion government in accordance with the request of the provincial government;
And whereas before executing said interim license the government of Canada desires to have same approved of by the government of Manitoba;
And whereas it appears expedient for the government of Manitoba to approve of said interim license;
On the recommendation of the honourable the minister, the committee advise-
That said interim license be and it is hereby approved and that the Minister of the Interior be requested to execute the same.
I do not know of any transaction which could be more within the statute than that, and I cannot understand why that transaction should be invoked in an endeavour to support the resolution now before this house proposing to take out of the hands of the government the right to execute licenses under the Dominion Water Powers Act. It has been suggested already what would be the situation in Alberta and Saskatchewan, and I only want to suggest what would be the situation in Nova Scotia, where for years the executive had the right to issue licenses for water-powers and for crown lands and where there never has been a suggestion that the legislature should pass on each individual act in that respect. As I said a moment ago, the only time the legislature would be called upon to act would be in case of the transfer of the fee simple, the title to the natural resources.
Just one further word: It seems to me that we have lost sight of the fact that some days ago this house adopted a resolution moved by the hon. member for Frontenac-Adding-ton (Mr. Edwards) and seconded by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) stating:
That, in the opinion of this house, in the best interests of confederation, and the economic development of western Canada, the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta should be granted their natural resources-
What we are doing here, and what has been done, is to endeavour to expedite that transfer as far as could be done under the statute as it stood. What has been done is this:	It
has been agreed by this House of Commons that it is now our policy to transfer to the western provinces their natural resources. In July of last year this government, believing this policy would be adopted by the House of Commons, entered into an agreement which it expected would be ratified by this house,

Natural Resources-Mr. Ralston
and I take it that that agreement has been ratified through the adoption of this resolution. In connection with that agreement it was not proposed to wait until actual legislation was passed when the government had already the power in connection with an individual case to grant a license, but to exercise that power according to the wishes of the province for which the federal government from that time on held the property; and so the license was granted to the province of Manitoba pursuant to that arrangement, in the spirit of the resolution which was adopted by this house, in an attempt in good faith to grant to the province of Manitoba those natural resources which everyone agrees should go back to them.
With regard to the contract itself, very little attempt has been made to criticize it in any way, and really one finds it difficult to understand just why we have taken so long in this debate in view of that fact, because after all the merits of the contract itself should have something to do with this question. If it could be shown that the government had made an absolutely wretched contract, one which could not be defended, there might be some ground for taking some action in this house, but hardly a voice has been raised to suggest that the contract has been anything but proper and good for the province of Manitoba. By that contract the Pinarwa development was to be discontinued and 50,000 extra horse-power has been reclaimed and made available to the power users of Manitoba; by the contract 30,000 horse-power will be supplied the province at a rate of between $11 and $13 per horse-power, and under the contract the rates are made subject to the provincial public utilities board, so there is no danger that the people of that province will have to pay too much for power. Let me read section 14 of the contract:
Subject to designation for that purpose by the Governor in Council as required by paragraph (m) of section 12 of the act, the rates to be charged by the licensee for the power developed under this interim license shall be subject to and under the jurisdiction of the Municipal and Public Utility Board of the province of Manitoba, or its successor, and the said board shall have complete jurisdiction from time to time to fix just and reasonable rates to be charged by the said licensee determined in accordance with the provisions of the regulations.
Further than that, the following provision is made for taking over by the government of Manitoba itself:
Subject to the approval at the governor in council after notice of taking over has been given, His Majesty in the right of the province of Manitoba shall have the right to take over the final license at Seven Sisters falls, together
with all rights, powers, privileges, benefits and advantages in connection therewith, and all the works, lands and properties of the licensee at said Seven Sisters falls used by said licensee for the production of electrical energy thereat, in accordance with the conditions set out in section 11 of the said agreement of April 25, 1928.
I will just place before the house one other provision of the agreement which seems to me rather important. As I said a moment ago, this agreement was made with the idea in view that the natural resources were to be returned to the province of Manitoba. That means that the reversion in this license would eventually be transferred to the province of Manitoba as soon as authority was granted by this parliament; in other words the province of Manitoba would become the landlord, the person granting the license, and the body owning the fee simple. Paragraph (i) of section 10 is as follows:
Notwithstanding any provisions of the regulations or of this license there shall upon the return of the natural resources to the province of Manitoba be paid by the licensee to the province of Manitoba for such provincial hydroelectric or other purposes as the lieutenant-governor in council of the province of Manitoba may determine such additional annual rentals per horse-power as the lieutenant-governor in council may determine by any general waterpower regulations.
In other words, when the natural resources are actually handed over to the province of Manitoba and the province becomes the licensor to this company, because of the fact that it will take the place of the federal government, then under this section the province of Manitoba is entitled to impose upon the company such additional rentals as the lieutenant-governor in council of that province may see fit. That means that the company is under the control of the province in connection with the rates to be paid for power. The rates of the company are to be regulated by the public utilities commission of the province, and in addition to that the amount the company is to pay for rentals to be fixed by the lieutenant governor in council. It seems to me that should pretty well protect the public interest; and when we have the added fact that this license was granted on the request of the province of Manitoba itself it seems to me that we have to all intents and purposes public control and public ownership in just as full and free a sense as if the license had been granted to the province of Manitoba itself.
May I just say one thing more, and it is not in connection with the lease which is the subject of this debate. It arises from what was said by the hon. member for Frontenae-
656	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Ralston
Addington, who, in a very whimsical speech, put forth his ideas with regard to the constitutional question as to natural resources. I do not wish to raise a legal discussion in the house at this late hour, but I must say that I cannot, either as- a member of this house or as a professional man, agree with the legal opinion expressed by the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington. I hardly think he will find that the western provinces themselves will rely upon the argument he put forward.

Nearly all the sections of the British North America Act, the Alberta Act and the Manitoba Act were cited, and the hon. member was setting himself up, for the time being at least, as the chief justice of the court on constitutional principles. I do not think the western provinces will associate themselves with the contention he made, which was to this effect: It is true that when we came into confederation we got a certain payment in lieu of lands, but we now find that you had no right constitutionally and technically to withhold our lands; therefore we suggest that we should have the money in lieu of lands and the lands too. That was the argument of the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington, and I only desire to go on record as stating that I cannot agree with any such contention. The real contention is rather that this matter should be considered on broad and equitable principles and the natural resources handed over to the western provinces on that ground and not in this narrow and to say the least highly technical argument. If I am correctly informed, that is the position which is being taken by the province of Manitoba in connection with the hearing which is going on before the commission.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that neither the resolution nor the amendment to the resolution should be supported'. I believe they lay down a principle which has never before been laid down in connection with the administration of public property. It has always been considered the responsibility of the executive to look after these matters, and the remedy is not that of taking away from the executive the power which is vested in them in the usual course of constitutional practice.
