speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been drawn into this argument more by accident than by design.
I chanced to make a remark during the course of the speech of the Minister of Railways (Mr. 
Dunning), and immediately the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) took very decided and I thought rather strenuous objection to my remark. Therefore, I feel called upon to make clear to the house the understanding upon which that remark was made.
Before doing so, let me be careful to say that so far as I am concerned I have not been very much interested in the fight which has been going on between certain members of the house and the Minister of the Interior. I do not understand the exact situation in Manitoba and I do not care to offer any comment on the misunderstandings which have developed in connection with the Seven Sisters falls in that province. It would appear to me that no matter how much the Minister of the Interior may or may not be involved in the matter, the government of Manitoba must accept whatever blame may befall in this connection. But when it comes to the amendment which is before the house there is a principle involved which I most heartily endorse, and I intended to vote for the amendment without any speech at all. However, the objection of the minister, to which I have already referred, makes it necessary for me to offer an explanation.
During the Prime Minister's speech on this question I understood him to say that it was the policy of this government to treat the provinces which had not yet obtained their natural resources as if they had always had them. That was his statement as I understood it, but when the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) was speaking he not only made some extravagant claims for the application of the resolution to the natural resources in other provinces, but he made the statement that the Minister of the Interior had been treating all provincial governments alike in respect to their water-powers and natural resources. I took exception to that because I knew for a fact that the government of Alberta had been endeavouring for a considerable time to get control of the Spray lakes power site. The position of the Minister of the Interior in respect to Spray lakes has been this:-if I am mistaken he will correct me-he refuses to give a lease of that power site to the Alberta government unless they will assure this government that they intend to operate that plant as a government undertaking. That is the understanding I have, and if the minister denies it of course I shall have to withdraw the remark I made.

I am glad to have this explanation from the minister, but he must recognize that the conditions he has submitted to the government of Alberta are impossible ones. I will not go into the details of that because it would require more engineering knowledge than I have at my command at the moment. Until very recently I had not seen any published statement from the minister or from the Alberta government that the conditions under which this power site might be taken over by the government had been altered by the minister. I take his word, but prior to a short time ago it is clear that he had not been treating those two provinces in precisely the same way. Those were the grounds upon which I put the query to the Minister of Railways.
Let me come now to the amendment as it may affect the Spray lakes. Supposing, say ten years from now, there is still a squabble between the provincial government and the 78594-42
Dominion government as to whether a certain number of cubic feet or something else shall be guaranteed or not in the Spray lakes proposition. Some kind of squabble has taken place and lasted, and the result is that the provincial government has not control. I am just afraid that something similar might happen to that power site to what has happened in the case of the Seven Sisters falls in Manitoba. True, the minister says to parliament now that he will guarantee that nothing shall be disposed of without the wish of the province of Alberta. I do not want to insinuate anything, but that was pretty much what I understood him to say last year and it might happen that an excuse could be developed. I am not saying that the minister needs an excuse but if he needs one he has made a very excellent excuse, I must say. It might happen subsequently that conditions would render it possible for the minister to make the same disposition of Spray lakes as has happened in Manitoba. Therefore, in order to prevent that kind of thing, since this power plant is in the national parks, the amendment has great point and force.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
At the present time the disposal of this power site is, as I understand the matter, in the hands of the minister, and while I have a considerable amount of respect for the minister, nevertheless I would like to get the assurance of parliament that this site and others in a similar position would not be given away by a minister without at least a discussion in parliament in respect thereto.
I listened a few minutes ago to the hairsplitting legal distinctions of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). I think I was able to follow his argument, and I think, too, it was only occasionally he came within range of the subject. He says that the disposition of water-power is a matter of administration; that being a matter of administration, it should not be interfered with by any limiting resolution of the character of the one now before the house. He says furthermore that, it being a matter of administration, wThv, we can come back to parliament and have a row with the minister as we are having now, that we can come back to parliament and we can lay all kinds of charges against the minister. That is rather a peculiar kind of argument. Just imagine

65S

Natural Resources-Mr. Irvine
forty years from now when our children are paying a very high price for electric energy, they will turn up Hansard and as a consolation for having to pay that high price, read what the minister says! Can you imagine them saying: Never mind; pay the high price; they had a row with the minister over making that contract? Is that a good argument? That, however, is precisely the meaning of the minister's argument. It is all very well to come here and make insinuations to a minister after he has done the deed, if he has done it, having of course, no reference at all to the present minister. That may be a great satisfaction for an individual on the floor of parliament in 1929 but it is a rather poor argument for those who, forty years from now, will have to pay a high price for power under the control of a private company. That is what we are trying to safeguard.
Then the Minister of National Defence comes to the last extremity of his defence- and only a minister of defence could think of such an argument. He says: "Mr. Speaker and hon. members of the house, surely something ought to be said for the contract; surely if it is a good contract, that ought to excuse the minister and the government of Manitoba and anybody else for anything that might have happened. Suppose somebody steals the watch from the pocket of the minister tonight when he is going home. Of course I do not. say that the word "stealing" is applicable to the Seven Sisters; there is no reference to such a thing. But suppose to-morrow morning the gentleman who steals the watch of the hon. gentleman turns out to be a fine looking fellow and so we bring him into court and we say: "Now, don't be too hard on this gentleman; see how good looking he is, a fine stalwart fellow with a bald head and a mustache; a man *who can hold his head up anywhere." Is that an excuse for his stealing the watch? His good looks has just as much to do with his stealing the watch as the minister's argument has to do with the question before the house or as the contract of the Winnipeg Electric has to do with the charges against the Minister of the Interior. No matter how good the contract was, it went to a private company and those who have been fighting for a principle, who believe in public development, think they have made a claim that the minister in some way or another broke faith with them. As to that I have no remarks to make, but I would say that the minister's ingenious argument did not have much to do with the amendment before the house.
Finally, I think the Prime Minister's argument was a strange one from our own

Prime Minister who has been on the public platform the champion of parliamentary institutions to a more outstanding degree than any other public man I can remember in the history of Canada. I was reading just to-day the bible of the Liberal party. I do not know sir, whether you have seen it, but it is a real bible with the bust of the Prime Minister on the front page and a really biblical quotation from a great Liberal somewhere across the Atlantic. In that bible there are some very definite pronouncements in respect to the power of parliament and there are some very specific references to the orders in council which were passed by the administration prior to the present one. The whole righteous indignation of a great Liberal party which has fought for the liberties of the Canadian people throughout our history was aroused to the very highest pitch in denouncing that kind of thing and promising to the people of Canada that if ever a Liberal party should come into power, all those rights and privileges of the people would be safeguarded by upholding parliamentary institutions and giving parliament the rights which belong to it properly in considering every question which concerns the interests of the people. That is a splendid principle. I am sure the Prime Minister still believes in that principle, but his argument does not fit in. I should say that his speech on this question indicated a profound disbelief in parliamentary institution. I hope he has not had a change of mind; I hope I am misinterpreting him on the question, because I think it would be nothing short of a calamity were the Prime Minister so soon to have lost the ideals which no doubt went a long way towards giving him the confidence of the people which he now enjoys. The parliament of Canada, if this confidence is to bn restored, must deal with matters so important to the welfare of the people as water-power.
Referring again to the administration argument of the Minister of National Defence, when those powers were granted by parliament who then thought of the importance of a river from a power point of view? Who then thought of the importance of electrical energy in the industrial development of the world? Nobody. Since that time electrical "nergy has become the greatest industrial motive force that we have, and consequently we might very properly make an exception in the administration of this particular natural resource. That is all that the amendment proposes. It makes a specific exception of water-powers because of their importance, and insists that before any water-power within the control of this government be given to any private company,

Natural Resources-Mr. Bancroft
parliament shall decide upon the question. That principle I uphold, and I shall therefore be glad to vote for the amendment.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
At this late hour I shall not delay the house at any great length, but there are a few remarks that I shou'd like to make in opposition to the resolution and the amendment now before the house. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, no disposition of the natural resources, under the control of the federal government, shall be effective until ratified by parliament.
The amendment strikes out the words "natural resources," and substitutes therefor the words "water-powers."
In my judgment both the resolution and the amendment are aimed at the natural resources and water-powers of the three prairie provinces. I shall speak more particularly of the province of Manitoba.
The water-powers of Manitoba are very, very valuable. The Winnipeg and "Nelson rivers are the chief sources of the water-powers of Manitoba. Winnipeg river drains lac Seul and the lake of the Woods into lake Winnipeg. This great river, falling over the rocky slopes on the western end of the Laurentians. creates a great amount of water-power, about three-quarters of a million horse-power.
The Nelson river, which flows from lake Winnipeg into Hudson bay, is four hundred miles long, and falls seven hundred feet in its course. This river is capable of producing somewhere around three and a half million horse-power. The people of Manitoba are very proud of these natural resources. They feel that these water-powers are their own property, that they belong to the people of Manitoba, and that no one else is directly concerned in their development or disposal.
The water-powers of Ontario have been developed or disposed of by the government of that province, representing the people of Ontario. The water-powers of Quebec have been developed or disposed of by the government of that province, representing the people of Quebec. Both these provinces have seen fit to develop and dispose of their water-powers without consulting the federal parliament. They never thought of consulting the Canadian senate. Yet if this resolution and amendment carry to-night, the people of Manitoba cannot develop their water-powers without first coming and consulting the federal members in this house from Ontario and Quebec, from the island of Cape Breton and from the Yukon, and if they succeed in convincing the majority of these members that their plans are good, next they have to run the gauntlet of the Canadian senate before they can proceed to develop what they believe to be their own water-pow'ers. I cannot understand how any member from Manitoba, and this applies to the members from the other prairie provinces as well, can vote for a resolution Which places the people of the province of Manitoba in an inferior position, as compared with the older provinces, in the matter of developing their natural resources. Surely the rights of the people of Manitoba are not less than the rights of the people of the older provinces. If they are, it is high time we knew about it.
Not much more than a week ago the house unanimously passed a resolution moved by the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) declaring, in effect, that in the best interests of confederation, and the economic development of -western Canada, the three western provinces should be granted their natural resources free from restrictions. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) supported that resolution, and in view of his action then I cannot understand how he can now move a resolution which places a restriction upon the return of the natural resources to the prairie provinces. The whole house approved of the return to the provinces of those resources. The hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), the acting leader of the opposition, who moved the amendment now before the house, supported the resolution of the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington, and yet his amendment would place a very serious restriction upon the development of the natural resources of the western provinces.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I should just like to remind the hon. member that the resolution to which he refers has not yet been acted upon by this government.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I did not say anything about the action of this government. I do not know anything about the action of the government on this resolution. I said that the resolution had been accepted unanimously by the house.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: But until it is acted on by the government, this parliament is responsible for the natural resources.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
How can you expect a
government to act within two days?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
The resolution moved
by the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington declared that the natural resources of the western provinces should be returned to them without any strings attached, but if the resolution and the amendment now before the house passes, the resources of the western provinces
660	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Bancrojt
will not only have strings attached to them but they will be " roped and hog tied " by the other provinces. The amendment now before the house represents the Conservative policy on the question of the natural resources. Provincial rights are to be over-ridden, restrictions and limitations are to be imposed upon the prairie provinces. The development of the natural resources is to be subject to the whims of this house and of the senate.
The policy of this government with respect to the natural resources was clearly stated by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on Thursday night. Speaking on this resolution the right hon. the Prime Minister said:
Water-power to-day is coming to have a significance in industrial development which it has never bad heretofore in the history of this country. The people of western Canada, appreciating that fact and realizing what it means to have possession of their water-powers, are anxious to have those water-powers under their own control to further in the manner they think best the industrial development of their provinces.
A little later on in the same speech he outlines the government's policy:
This government took the position that the right thing to do was to say that we believed the western provinces should be put as nearly as possible in exactly the position they would have been in had they had their resources from the moment they were created as provinces. That is the position we have taken in this new agreement; it admits of no debate or doubt, and having taken that position we intend to stand by it. We intend to see that the western provinces obtain their natural resources on a basis which will put them, so far as may now he possible, in the position they would have been in had they had the administration of their natural resources from the time they were created as provinces, and that means the right for their government and legislatures, not our parliament to decide what is to be done.
There can be no doubt which of these policies will appeal to the western provinces.
During the discussion of this resolution the Minister of the Interior has been severely criticized for his action with regard to the lease of the Seven Sisters falls power site. Some hon. members have said that after the Manitoba federal members had decided by a vote of ten to four against the granting of the lease t-o the Winnipeg Electric Company, the minister went ahead with the deal. I might remind some of my hon. friends from the province that in a case like this it is just as well to be fair. There are seventeen members from Manitoba; ten and four do not make seventeen. The fact is that of the Manitoba members ten were opposed to, and seven were in favour of, the granting of the lease. This afternoon the minister expressed
fMr. Bancroft.]
a preference for the views of those members from the province who were supporting the government. Well, fourteen of them are behind the government. Of these fourteen, seven were in favour of, and seven opposed to, the lease. So I submit he could not get very much guidance from them in view of that difference of opinion.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit a question, does he think party considerations should govern the minister's decision in matters of this character, rather than national considerations?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
As I understand it, the
Minister of the Interior consulted the Manitoba members, and then ascertained the views of the provincial government. The provincial government is the only body that is directly responsible to the people of Manitoba. Having done so, he acted on the advice of the Manitoba government, It has been stated that the minister did not oonsult the Manitoba members. I was one of those consulted by him in that connection. To my knowledge he consulted eight of the Manitoba members. We agreed, that, owing to the natural resources agreement our responsibility in the matter had ceased. Some four or five others he did not need to consult for he knew they were in favour of the lease.
It has been stated that the Bracken government has got into difficulties over the granting of the lease to the Winnipeg Electric Company, and will probably be defeated. I travelled extensively through Manitoba during last fall, I met many people and I attended a number of farmers' conventions. As a result I am of the opinion-I may be wrong-that a large majority of the people of Manitoba are in favour of the present agreement. I believe it will be ratified by the legislature. In my judgment, if the Bracken government had been defeated during the turmoil of the last two weeks, the government that succeeded it, regardless of party, would have put through the same deal.
The amendment and the resolution in my judgment would put the people of the western provinces in an inferior position as compared with their fellow-citizens in the other provinces in the development of their natural resources, and for that reason, Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote against both.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) I had no intention of participating in this debate until quite recently. Some remarks from the other side of the house caused me to change my mind.

Natural Resources-Mr. Campbell
I realize that in so far as this is a domestic question in Manitoba there would be impropriety in discussing it in this house. I intend to discuss the question only from the federal viewpoint. As to whether or not the Bracken government committed sins of omission or sins of commission, that I realize is for the people of Manitoba to decide, and not for me as a member from the province of Saskatchewan. But, sir, those resources are still under the control of the federal government. It is not a question whether the province of Manitoba should control them or not. We are dealing with facts, not theories. I repeat, this government does control those resources, and the very agreement that has been the subject of so much discussion here was made between the federal government and the Winnipeg Electric Company or its subsidiary; the government of Manitoba really did not figure directly in the deal at all. Therefore I submit we are within our rights in discussing this matter from the federal standpoint.
I listened with a good deal of interest the other night to the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and I congratulate him on coming out as the chief protagonist in this house of provincial rights. I rather welcome his stand. But I recognize that while appearing in this role, conversely he was attempting to put those of us who are supporting the resolution and the amendment in the position of being opposed to provincial rights. Well, in so far as I am concerned, I am quite ready to be judged by the people of the prairie provinces. I am perfectly confident that the people of the three prairie provinces will not regard us as being opposed to provincial rights.
The Prime Minister argued rather speciously that if this amendment carried and agreements of this character had to be submitted to parliament they would have to pass a Tory senate. Of course that argument might have a good deal of effect in some quarters. I recall when not so many years ago the Prime Minister toured western Canada and made the welkin ring as he denounced that same Tory senate, and his indignation was so intense that he pledged himself on platform after platform at the then coming session of parliament to introduce legislation to reform the senate. But that happened many years ago, and the Prime Minister apparently has forgotten all about his promise. Let me tell him now that should there be any danger of the senate interfering as he suggests, if he will only carry out his promise to reform that branch of parliament he will relieve us of any occasion to worry about what a Tory senate may or may not do.
I do not consider that submitting any agreement to parliament for ratification is an infringement of provincial rights. It is an absolutely absurd suggestion, so absurd that it does not deserve attention. Surely the submission of any proposed alienation of these resources to parliament for ratification cannot by any stretch of imagination be considered an infringement of provincial rights. Suppose the government has decided to grant any of these natural resources to some company or to the provincial authorities, as the case may be, the government is in control of this house by reason of its majority, and therefore there is no reason why it should not submit its proposal to parliament for ratification. It could be done in this way just as well as by order in council.
One particular reason why I am in favour of the resolution and amendment is that their adoption would relieve the public mind of suspicion. There is no use denying the fact that from one end of the country to the other there is deep-rooted suspicion that there was something wrong with the Seven Sisters power site deal, that there was some ulterior motive behind the rather indecent haste both in Winnipeg and in Ottawa to alienate this very valuable water-power. I am not one of those who share these suspicions. I do not believe for a moment that there was anything wrong or dishonest in the transaction, either here at Ottawa or in the province of Manitoba. But I say that there are tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of people who will always believe that. If this agreement had been submitted to the legislature of Manitoba and submitted to parliament here, then the public mind would have been relieved, and it would have added to the dignity and prestige of parliament, which I must say has been impaired by this deal.
When the Prime Minister referred to the question of interference with provincial rights, I wondered whether he remembered the fact that it was only a few days ago that his associate, the Premier of Saskatchewan, had to break off negotiations with him and go home without those resources. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) made a great deal of the argument that the delay would hinder industrial development in the prairie provinces. I am just as anxious as he is to see a proper balance of industry in the prairies. I believe that the great industrial development which we shall see there in the next quarter of a century will relieve us of some of the troubles we have to bear at the present time and will bring about a better balance and create a home market. I am therefore just
662	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Campbell
anxious as any member in this house to see industrial development in the prairies. At the same time I think it is absurd to suggest that the submission of these agreements to parliament, so long as the federal government controls them, would seriously delay industrial development. Let me say, sir, that the basis of industrial development in the prairies as well as in other parts of Canada is cheap power, and if we give away these water-powers without any proper consideration of the public interest, we are doing the very thing which will delay, and seriously delay, industrial development in the future. If we aire looking into the future, if we are *considering those who will live in the country after we are dead and gone, if we want to see business and industry develop as it should develop, then I say that that is an added reason why we should be careful and should delay for a reasonable time in order to ensure that these resources are not dissipated but are properly handled so that those who are building up industry will not be taxed to such an extent as to render industrial development impossible. But when we consider the delay which the Minister of Railways suggests, I would remind him that the Canadian Pacific Railway must come to parliament for every branch line and every foot of railway it builds -

speechtext: No.

speechtext: -except yard increases.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is not
right. If the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other railway company desires to build a line of railway wholly within a province it can go to the provincial legislature.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
The argument is the
same; they must go to some parliament to have it done. That is my point. Does the minister say that this is going to hold up railway building? The Canadian National Railways must do the same. There are many classes of companies, insurance and financial companies, that must come to this parliament to be incorporated. Not only must they come to parliament to be incorporated but they must come here in order to get the right to increase their stock. Is that such a serious matter? I do not think it is, and that should not justify any indecent haste in disposing of these resources.
Then the minister refers to the conditions in the prairie provinces as compared with Ontario and Quebec. They are not analagous at all. If the prairie provinces controlled these resources, then it would be a matter for those provinces themselves to decide as to 
what is the proper way to alienate them; and with that we have nothing to do. But we are deciding to-day on resources that are still controlled by this parliament-resources in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.
Now the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) used, it seemed to me, some rather lemarkable arguments. He advanced as an argument why we should not pass this resolution the statement that the house had already placed itself on record and accepted unanimously a resolution in which the hope was expressed that the resources would be turned over to the prairie provinces. I believe that you, Mr. Speaker, some time ago referred to one such resolution as simply a pious hope. And that is all it is. Until that resolution is carried out and the resources are absolutely turned over, the question is simply an abstract one and means nothing.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: Does my hon. friend argue that until they are actually transferred we should pay no regard to the wishes of the provincial governments with respect to their disposition? Is that the argument?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I was not dealing with that argument at all; I was dealing with the suggestion that we should not pass this resolution because the house a few days ago had passed another resolution. I say that the other resolution is not in effect at the present time. It is true that the house accepted it, but the very fact that the minister's own former colleague, the Premier of Saskatchewan, and his colleagues, had to break off negotiations and go back home shows how ineffective that other resolution is to-day. Surely we are not going to refuse to consider these matters simply because that resolution- which, as I say, you, Mr. Speaker, would probably describe as a pious hope-was passed by the house a short time ago.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend does not answer the question. I stated to-night-and the hon. gentleman has criticized me in this regard-that ever since this government came into office there had been an increasing regard for the trusteeship feature of the relationship, and that the provincial governments had been consulted. Does my hon. friend object to that consultation? Does he object to our being guided, even under present circumstances, by the wishes of the provincial authorities?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
No, I certainly do not object to that at all.

Natural Resource's-Mr. Campbell

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: That is the whole point.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I do not object to that, but I say that the fact that a resolution has been passed with reference to the transfer of some resources does not constitute any reason why the present resolution should not be adopted; and if it were adopted it would relieve the public mind of a great deal of suspicion, all of which I believe is unjustified.
The minister referred to this very beautiful contract which has been drawn up. And it looks very beautiful until you begin to analyze it. But here you have a company tied up with an agreement under which the government of Manitoba can expropriate that power plant after thirty years. Now the minister knows perfectly well that inside thirty years that company would be so entrenched, it would have such power and influence in Manitoba as to be in a position to upset any government that dared try to exercise the right of expropriation. Through the control of newspapers, by means of contributions to party funds, and so forth, it would be absolutely impossible for any government inside thirty years to interfere with an interest of that kind.
The Minister of Railways said that he, while premier of Saskatchewan, had always been consulted in regard to any major disposal of natural resources. I was wondering whether he was consulted in regard to the disposal of a considerable block of land in 1924. Some 129,517 acres of land in the province of Saskatchewan were turned over to the Hudson's Bay Company in 1924. I hold in my hand a copy of sessional paper 101, a return asked for by one hon. member from Alberta. The question is asked whether the Hudson's Bay Company has obtained any grant of land's in Canada since 1921 and if so in what province, what districts in each province, the date of transfer, and by what authority these lands were transferred; and there is a list showing the disposal of 65,533 acres in Manitoba; 129,517 acres in Saskatchewan; and 153,924 acres in Alberta, making a grand total of 348,974. The authority for the deed of surrender is the Dominion Lands Act, and the order in council was passed on December 19, 1924. It is P.C. No. 2158, and the agreement between the crown and the Hudson's Bay Company was dated December 23, 1924. I believe perhaps this is one of the reasons why the Premier of Saskatchewan refused the offer to continue the present subsidy and receive back the natural resources. A very large part of our natural resources has been alienated already, and I think it would be absurd for the Premier of Saskatchewan to
accept the return of those resources without an accounting for what has been alienated in the past. I believe the Minister of Railways himself, if he occupied that responsible position to-day, would refuse to accept that proposition.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
A short time ago my
hon. friend asked whether I was consulted in connection with the settlement with the Hudson's Bay Company. I was not consulted, for the obvious reason contained in the report itself. That transfer was due to a settlement as to what were the terms of the original deed of surrender of 1867 from the Hudson s Bay Company to Canada. It was a matter of right and not a matter of giving something away.

I think perhaps the
minister will agree that this was a transfer of land to the Hudson's Bay Company in lieu of some release of land they made in the province of Alberta.

Can my hon. friend find
that in the documents?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: I have not the complete file here but certainly that is what I gather. The argument still exists: our resources have been alienated and I say the province is entitled to some accounting for them.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
To settle
the matter, may I say that the Hudson's Bay Company have not made absolutely final selections yet. They have been making selections for years to complete their agreement.

speechtext:
There is another matter to which I would like to refer, and that is the disposal of a large block of our school lands in Saskatchewan. This is a phase of the question which has not been dealt with during this debate. I hold in my hand a list of lands which will be offered for sale at Maple Creek, Saskatchewan, on Monday, March 18, 1929, and another list which will be offered for sale at Wolseley, Saskatchewan, on Wednesday, March 20, 1929. I wonder just what is the reason for the haste in disposing of these school lands. It seems to me positively absurd to hold a sale of school lands or any other kind of lands in the prairies in the month of March. There are various reasons j am opposed to this sale. First, I claim that this government has no legal right to offer the lands for sale. I take the view held 'by the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards), although the Minister of National Defence says he does not
664	COMMONS
Natural Resources-Mr. Campbell
agree with that view. It seems to me this government agreed with it, and that is the view expressed by Mr. Bram Thompson, a lawyer of Regina, who I think -was the first man to express that point of view. This government really accepted that principle in its dealings with Manitoba, and it seems to me they were influenced by that point of view in this transaction. So I say I am opposed to the sale of these lands because I do not think this government has any legal right to offer them for sale.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Will my hon.
friend permit a question?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I have only a few
moments to speak, and I must make the best use of them. There is really an over-production of wheat this year; the best statistical authority on this matter states that there is an over-production of 400,000,000 bushels. A few days ago I read an article in the Financial Times of Montreal, a paper which can hardly be accused of agitating the farmer in connection with his grievances, and in this article the opinion is expressed that the net return to the farmer on the prairie this year for his wheat was only fifty cents a bushel. I say that to a large extent that is due to overproduction, and' just at this time it is absurd to throw all this extra land on the market which will result in an increase in this overproduction.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Did my hon.
friend say the net return or the average return was 50 cents? Did he mean there would be a profit of 50 cents?

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
No, after the fanner
paid for his threshing the net return would be 50 cents a bushel, I would hesitate to quote any farm paper in that regard, but this opinion is expressed by the Financial Times of Montreal, so I say it is absurd to throw a lot more land on the market and further depress prices.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Without
desiring to interrupt my hon. friend, I may say that it is not usual to sell these lands in March, but this is being done at the request of the provincial government, and the sale itself is taking place under an agreement with the government.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext: May I ask whether the provincial government wanted the sale to take place in March?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Yes, and I will give the reason: They said they wished the sale to take place early so that the people 
purchasing the land might have plenty of time to farm it this season. That is the reason they gave me, although as I say we do not usually sell these lands in March.

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL THAT DISPOSITION BE EFFECTIVE ONLY ON APPROVAL OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
That is a poor reason,
because this is wild land and it must be broken up before it can be cropped. However, I am glad to hear the explanation; we will have to discuss this matter with the provincial government. It does seem to me, however, that with the tremendous increase in wheat acreage in the United States and the corresponding increase in Canada, due partly to immigration and partly to the combine in the west, this over-production will increase. In 1914 our acreage of wheat was only 10,000,000, while in 1928 it had increased to over 23,000,000 acres. The same laws of economics apply to the agricultural industry that apply to every other industry, although some people do not think so, and if your production is too great you will have a slump in the market. Look at the condition of the pulp and paper industry to-day; we have seen the premiers of Ontario and Quebec going to a great deal of trouble to get these mill owners to reduce their output, and finally they have reached an agreement. They considered it a national calamity because there was an over-production of pulp, but is it not an equally great calamity to have an over-production of wheat? The purchasing power of the farmers will be reduced this year by from $50,000,000 to $60,000,000 because of that overproduction, and at this time we are proposing to put this additional land on the market in order to grow more wheat and increase that surplus.
